Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”
Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.

While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.

Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.

“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”

The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.

To use the device, patients undergo an hour-long procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors.

“The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed under the in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where . . .it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.”

He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a there’s a next ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.”

When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired.

As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has previously said that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue.
The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors.

“In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.”

Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI. While the company isn’t designing for “healthy 40-year-olds,” he said, it believes people will eventually need some kind of BCI by the age of 60 or 70.
“We want to figure out how do we extend not just lifespan but health span,” Hodak said.
Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?

Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.

The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power

Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places.

Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? A brain implant changed her life. Then it was removed against her will.

Sticking an electrode inside a person’s brain can do more than treat a disease. Take the case of Rita Leggett, an Australian woman whose experimental brain implant changed her sense of agency and self. She told researchers that she “became one” with her device.
She was devastated when, two years later, she was told she had to remove the implant because the company that made it had gone bust.
Her case highlights the need for a new category of legal protection: neuro rights. Explore how they could be protected.

Katie Zacharia, the Trump administration’s new press secretary, did not have the greatest first day of work. Zacharia gave her first press briefing, which lasted just 14 minutes, on Tuesday, and it went so poorly that it reportedly left even Republicans wondering how long she’ll last.

Zacharia is taking over for Karoline Leavitt, who resigned in August and is now set to join Fox News. While Leavitt’s tenure as press secretary was marked by her hostility toward both the media and factual truth, she at least seemed comfortable in her position. Zacharia, on the other hand, stumbled through her introductions, which she appeared to read from a printed script. At one point, she accidentally referred to her husband as “my president.” She seemed to shock members of the media when she announced that the administration had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as ambassador to Greece. Outside of the briefing room, while she was answering questions with President Trump, a reporter asked where Zacharia passed the bar exam, and she responded with, “When I moved to China.”

To make matters worse, it seems that Zacharia does not have the unequivocal support of her Republican colleagues, per MS NOW. One anonymous White House official apparently admitted that she “got off on the wrong foot,” adding, “she needs to get much better, fast, otherwise she’ll break Scaramucci’s record.” (Anthony Scaramucci did a famously brief stint as the White House’s press secretary during Trump’s first administration in 2017 — he was dismissed after just 11 days.) Another official reportedly called the briefing “rough all around” and theorized that “The press and the administration are all probably thinking the same thing: we miss Karoline.”
But Trump, at least, “thought she was very good.”

Below is one of this spooky season’s biggest shows, literally: Set on the coast of Newfoundland, it relies on sweeping vistas of the Atlantic shoreline, massive icebergs hundreds of miles from where they belong, and something very, very big lurking under the water’s surface.

It’s also very familiar. Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: A tiny fishing village in the Northeast is beset by strange phenomena that leave people missing, mad, or dead, and only one desperate man and his friends can stop the horror. That’s right, it’s also roughly the premise of Widow’s Bay, not to mention the dozens of Stephen King and H.P. Lovecraft stories and imitations that inspired it. And while Widow’s Bay operates in a comedic register that Below doesn’t possess (at least not intentionally), it’s hard to watch this new series without comparing it to its Emmy-festooned recent predecessor given their many narrative, character, and setting overlaps. So with all six episodes of Below now streaming on Netflix, we’re taking a survey of how creator Jesse McKeown’s and star Josh Hartnett’s Canadian maritime monster party stacks up against Katie Dippold’s New England horror comedy. In this cross-border, cross-streamer rivalry, which is the real village of the damned good television?
Warning: Spoilers for Below and Widow’s Bay lie ahead.

Below stars Josh Hartnett as Calvin Penney, a fisherman fallen on hard times who now retrieves chunks of floating Arctic ice to be used in making vodka and reluctantly AirBnBs his home to tourists. As a child, Calvin was resettled to the Newfoundland town of Snook’s Arm from the tiny island of Little Pot Rock by the Canadian government as a cost-saving measure. When his family was towing the house by boat to the new location, something pulled it down into the depths with Calvin’s father trapped inside. All young Calvin sees, or thinks he sees, is a giant eyeball in the water. When strange things begin happening years later, Calvin raises the alarm.

Widow’s Bay stars Matthew Rhys as Tom Loftis, mayor of a cursed island off the coast of an unnamed state that it’s safe to assume is Maine, which Tom is now trying to promote as a tourist destination. Tom too lost family to the waters off the coast: His wife, a native islander, was stricken by a stroke — and, it’s implied, by the island’s curse — as she was trying to leave Widow’s Bay while pregnant.

As one of Below’s chief doomsayers, Hartnett’s Calvin combines Rhys’s leading-man energy with the salty-old-coot vibes of Mayor Tom’s nemesis turned ally, Wyck (Stephen Root), the town’s eccentric harbormaster. Two roles in one earns you some extra points. Plus his tragic maritime backstory involves a literal sea monster.
The Quirky but Competent Heroine With Something to Prove

Below co-stars Mackenzie Davis as Dr. Fonda Howander (what a name!), a marine biologist studying the regional waters with dismay as climate change wreaks havoc on the ecosystem. Despite her adorkable personality, it’s her knowledge that clues Calvin into what they’re dealing with and how to avoid getting killed by it. In the end, her steely resolve saves Snook’s Arm from disaster.

Widow’s Bay co-stars Kate O’Flynn as Patricia Moyer, a social outcast who works as Tom’s assistant and is convinced no one likes her — in part because very few people do. Despite her comically neurotic personality, it’s her dogged determination that helps piece together the mystery of the island. In the end, her steely resolve saves Widow’s Bay from disaster.

Davis is a fine actor, but her job here is primarily to deliver exposition with wide-eyed wonder and be awkward around the hunky Calvin. We’ve seen this kind of character before. Patricia? One of a kind. (“It’s the way you’re saying it.”)

Below’s supporting cast is primarily family. Charlie Heaton makes an impression as Wade, Calvin’s chipper but deeply frustrated failson. So does Willow Kean as Ruth, Calvin’s no-nonsense older sister and Snook’s Arm’s harbormaster. (What a boom time for harbormasters on television!) It’s never stated outright, but Ruth appears to be in a throuple with two perfectly nice people in their 50s, and everyone seems fine with it. So that’s interesting!

Widow’s Bay’s supporting cast includes just about every beloved American TV character actor known to man: Root, Dale Dickey, Kevin Carroll, Jeff Hiller, Toby Huss, Betty Gilpin, and Hamish Linklater are among the highlights.
Sorry, but that murderers’ row of unpretentious acting talent isn’t going to be topped.

Perhaps even more than the gigantic thing swimming in the ocean eating people, the thick Newfoundland accents are Below’s standout feature. There’s a lilt to them that leaves one tourist commenting that they feel like they’re in Ireland. The accents help make Snook’s Arm feel like a place out of time, just because it’s so unusual to hear that kind of speech in North America anyplace other than right there.

Meanwhile, not a single main character on Widow’s Bay does a Down-Easter accent, even though the show’s main inspiration, Stephen King, has for literally decades been writing characters who have it. You’re telling me Root couldn’t manage a single “ayuh”?
While it’s up for debate how well Hartnett, Davis, and Heaton pull off their respective attempts (sound off in the comments!), the effort has to count for something, right?

We’ve waded around this long enough: Below is about a giant squid. A real giant squid, a leviathan of the deep, a relic of eons past that attacks boats, docks, cars, houses, Portuguese sailing vessels, billionaires’ submersibles, tourists who camp too close to the shoreline, a goddamned moose, you name it.

The only real trace we get of the sea monster off Widow’s Bay is in a story Wyck tells Tom about his youth, in which his best friend was carried away by a tentacled beast we only hear about and never see. (There’s always season two, of course.)
I can’t stress this enough: This show is about a gigantic berserk squid, and it gets a lot of screen time, too!

Oh, you thought a giant squid would be the extent of Below’s paranormal activity? After coming into contact with the squid, Wade begins to have visions of the hag, a black-haired, sopping-wet woman in white who comes to him repeatedly. At first, she seems to be just a nightmarish apparition, but then late in the season, we learn she has lured Wade away … to Little Pot Rock, the island Calvin came from, where she lives in his somehow resurfaced home with her father and grandfather. Below’s detour to Little Pot Rock wraps up quickly with little explanation for the erstwhile hag’s seemingly flesh-and-blood existence on the island, but something spooky’s going on with her for sure.

The sea hag in Widow’s Bay, by contrast, is a monstrous cross between Samara from The Ring, the entity from It Follows, and the lady in the bathtub from The Shining. She kills you by sitting on your face but can be momentarily disadvantaged if you know the right time to tilt back your recliner.

The Below’s squid secretes a poisonous psychoactive substance that triggers flulike symptoms and intense dehydration, driving those who suffer from it into the sea to drown in an attempt to quench their thirst.

On Widow’s Bay, Patricia falls under the influence of an evil book that brainwashes her into making a party punch with animal blood, putting her guests into a trance during which they all walk into the water to drown. (They’re saved at the last moment, and fortunately, no giant squid lives off Widow’s Bay to eat them.)

In both cases, it’s deeply disturbing to watch people lose control of their minds and offer themselves up to the sea. However, in only one of these cases does the culprit wear a cool antler headdress and take drink recipes from the Necronomicon.

Widow’s Bay is best summed up by a quote from Karl Marx (seriously): “The tradition of all dead generations weighs like a nightmare on the brains of the living.” Tom, Patricia, Wyck, and the rest of the townsfolk and tourists are stuck dealing with a hell on earth created by their ancestors, who forged and maintained the deal with the Devil that makes the island what it is.

Below is a straight-up climate-change allegory. In fact, it’s not even an allegory: Climate change is what sends the ice drifting down from the Arctic and, with it, the giant squid. Characters talk about it in so many words, often. It’s the whole reason the fishing economy has collapsed, forcing Calvin to search for ice to begin with. It’s the point of Dr. Howander’s job. It’s what the show’s about. Well, that and a rampaging giant squid.

Both shows have pointed messages about the mess we’re in, and both end on a cliffhanger promising more horrors to come, but only Below’s cliffhanger implies the collapse of the Arctic ice shelf (not to mention a second season of this supposed limited series).

Below is a super-fun creature feature, a climate-aware cross between a kaiju film, a Stephen King story, Jaws, and Jurassic Park. But its ambitions largely stop there. Even though the two shows have different aims despite their similarities, Below can’t help but suffer in comparison to the perfectly balanced horror-comedy masterpiece that is Widow’s Bay, which feels like a precognitive parody of this series specifically.

Dunking on Below on behalf of Widow’s Bay, however, feels like missing the point of Widow’s Bay. That show isn’t a Walk Hard–style act of beheading its genre; it’s an active example of that genre that actually pulls off the kind of small Northeastern coastal-town horror it riffs on. Widow’s Bay doesn’t tell you that stories like Below are bogus, it proves how much fun they can be. In its own earnest, tentacled way, Below proves it too.

Just a few weeks from the end of the 2026 midterm elections, there are all sorts of variables that could affect the outcome on the margins. There remain many races for House, Senate, and governorships that are very close. Polling errors could be painting an unduly rosy picture of Democratic prospects. Late ad blitzes or candidate debates may tilt the balance here and there. “October surprises” remain a possibility, or even a “November surprise” by way of Trump-administration efforts to suppress or intimidate voters.

But the basic national dynamics of this election seem very clear. Midterms are always to a considerable extent referenda on the job performance and character of whoever occupies the White House. In Donald Trump, we have a highly controversial president who is the dominant personality of our era, with a record that is drawing terrible reviews from the public. His current job-approval ratio per the RealClearPolitics polling averages is 38.1 percent approval and 59.5 percent disapproval. Presidents with this level of unpopularity almost always post big midterm losses. But he also has a virtually unshakable hard core of supporters. As a party, Democrats have made their campaign a consistent frontal assault on Trump’s most vulnerable point — his poor record on, and his contemptuous disinterest in, high and rising living costs — with important sub-themes stressing the corruption that has flourished in his administration and deploring his war of choice against Iran. For their part, Republicans have mostly focused on energizing Trump’s most loyal supporters and maximizing their turnout, while trying to get more skeptical voters to think about their misgivings toward the opposition.

Let’s be clear about one thing: Trump’s energize-the-base tactics aren’t going to win the midterms. These voters are already energized. Yes, slightly increasing their turnout can help staunch the bleeding and keep down Democratic gains in deep-red territory. But even if the president gets them whipped up into a frenzy, there aren’t enough of them to overwhelm super-energized Democrats plus the vast and largely alienated ranks of swing voters who don’t like Trump’s economy or Trump’s war and are generally tired of his act.

But the shred of hope for a less-than-disastrous GOP result (defined as holding onto the Senate and holding Democrats to a small majority in the House) stems from the battle over a more strategic slice of the electorate: non-MAGA folk who voted for Trump in 2024. Many are standard-brand Republicans who never drank the Kool-Aid. Others are independents who were unhappy with Biden’s own economic record and remembered Trump’s first term as relatively prosperous. Some, though not many, were even Democrats weary of the octogenarian president or of this or that annoying party faction.

But however they got themselves into Trump’s column in 2024, many are up for grabs this year and his party is still losing ground. A large new Pew survey released last week shows that only 67 percent of verified 2024 Trump voters approve of the job he’s doing as president. This percentage drops to 57 percent among Latino voters, and 49 percent of under-30 voters, who backed Trump in 2024. Similarly the latest Economist-YouGov weekly tracking poll shows 21 percent of 2024 Trump voters disapprove of his job performance, a number that drops to 7 percent among self-identified MAGA supporters.

The drop-off among non-MAGA 2024 Trump voters largely explains the big picture. In 2024, Republicans won the presidential popular vote by 1.5 percent and the national House popular vote by 2.6 percent. According to the RCP averages, they trail in the generic congressional ballot (an estimation of the national House popular vote) by 7.9 percent at present (the margin is 9 percent at Silver Bulletin and 8.5 percent at Decision Desk HQ). That’s a loss of over 10 percent in vote share. Losing a big chunk of your coalition from the last election will do that to you. And it doesn’t help that Republicans are also losing among those who did not vote at all in 2024 (a mix of 2024 couch potatoes and new 2026 voters). Pew shows them breaking Democratic by about a 3-to-2 margin.

While parading Trump around to play the old hits and bellow about his accomplishments isn’t likely to help Republicans close the gap, the GOP tactic of relentlessly and expensively attacking Democrats could gain some traction, precisely because many alienated 2024 Trump voters aren’t sold on the opposition either. The Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter recently zeroed in on the GOP’s challenge:

[W]hile Trump tries to rally his base with calls to vote “like I’m on the ballot”, a recent Echelon Insights poll taken for Puck News illustrates just how much the MAGA/Trump coalition has splintered since 2024. In January of 2025, writes Puck’s Peter Hamby, “59 percent of Republicans identified more with Trump, while 36 percent identified with the party. Now? Only 34 percent of Republicans consider themselves primarily a supporter of Trump, versus 56 percent who say they support the G.O.P.”
In other words, the challenge for the GOP this cycle isn’t to get Trump voters to the polls; it’s getting non-MAGA identified voters to show up.

Ideally for Republicans to turn back the “blue wave,” they’d need Trump to take a back seat and use their vast resources to whale away at Democrats, individually and collectively. The hope would be to break even in a war between excited base voters and close to half of the others who bother to vote deciding Republicans are the lesser of evils. So instead of Trump telling voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” Republicans should be telling voters to pretend he’s far away.

Unfortunately for the GOP, Trump can no more step to the rear of the stage than the sun can turn off its blinding light. His constant, abrasive presence will operate as a drag on late Republican campaign tactics, perhaps reminding his party that national elections are won by normal pols appealing to normal people.
The sharp stab of a bee sting hurts bad enough, but it's the venom that makes the pain last.

The stingers of honeybees (Apis mellifera) are typically single-use. In the process of stabbing their target's skin, the bee's stinger is ripped from its rear, leaving a considerable wound that the bee later dies from.
But even after the doomed bee has flown away, the stinger keeps on pumping.
As part of a new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, scientists have captured a disembodied stinger in action to better understand how they work.
It's a little disturbing, but also we can't look away. See for yourself in the video below.

"If you've ever been stung by a bee, you'll know it's a very painful process, but now we've been able to identify all the working parts packed into the tiny stinger," says entomologist Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel of Macquarie University in Australia.
"We've known since as early as 1910 that the venom sac of a honeybee stinger empties into a chamber with little pumping elements called valves, but until now we didn't know exactly how they work."
High-speed cameras captured the semi-translucent stinger as it plunges into a clear gel designed to mimic human skin, revealing the inner workings of this remarkable piece of biological machinery.

"Despite sustained interest in the hymenopteran stinger, to date no direct observations of the venom pumping exist and our understanding of the biomechanics of venom delivery remains limited," the team writes.
"The stinger of the honey bee has unique properties including being reasonably large, translucent, and being able to autotomize [disconnect from the bee's body] during stinging."
It's surprising nobody has done this already, because there's some really wild stuff going on inside.
Ramirez-Esquivel and team describe the stinger mechanism as a "unique double-piston micro-pump."
They used forceps to guide the stinger into place, but then a pair of sharp barbs called lancets take over, with alternating jabs that drive the barb further into the 'skin' while also pumping venom.

Each lancet is attached to a corresponding valve inside the bulb chamber – that's the thicker part at the base of the stinger. These flexible valves alternately inflate to drive their attached lancet down, and deflate to retract it, squeezing past each other as they alternate.
This also creates a downward pumping pressure on the connected venom chamber, drawing the liquid down towards the 'skin'.
"Finally, and perhaps most dramatically, as the valves meet in the middle of the stroke, they change shape again to push past each other," says Ramirez-Esquivel.

"This is a remarkable strategy to pump fluid since maintaining a seal is vital to effectively transmit pressure. The unique geometry of the valves is the key; they act as collapsible pistons and – by pumping in opposite directions – they're able to deliver a continuous flow of venom."

As far as we know, this autonomous pumping 'design' is unique to worker honey bees. It's never been seen before; other members of the order Hymenoptera achieve their stings with wave-like contractions around the venom tract, a bit like how our gut pumps food through our body.

The honeybee sting, on the other hand, is more similar to many human-made devices, like the syringes we use to inject drugs. Even these have only one relatively rigid piston in the chamber, which means they can't refill without creating backflow. Perhaps the bee stinger could inspire a device that can, for medical or research purposes.
"The double piston design adds complexity but it's the key to the stinger being able to deliver venom continuously in a compact, autonomous unit," says Ramirez-Esquivel.
The research has been published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The Space Force has officially established its component to U.S. Special Operations Command, creating a ninth component charged with presenting space expertise to commanders in the field.

The service activated the component Oct. 7, according to a Sept. 29 memo confirmed to be authentic by Air & Space Forces Magazine, and it plans to hold a formal ceremony in the coming weeks. The Space Force has had a special forces element operating at SOCOM headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base, Fla., but not a formal component field command.

The announcement comes more than 18 months after U.S. Special Operations Command revealed plans to create a space component. Congress pressed pause on that process in the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, blocking funding for the move until the Space Force provided more details on its plans.
A Space Force spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions about who would lead the component or provide details on its organizational structure. Axios first reported on the activation.

Space capabilities and forces have played a critical role in recent operations, according to senior defense officials. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine identified space forces as a “first mover” during the early days of Operation Epic Fury. And in a speech last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess highlighted electronic warfare operations performed by Guardians deployed with the Space Force’s 42nd Electronic Warfare Detachment, which supports U.S. Central Command and Space Forces Central.

Standing up components under every unified combatant command has been a focus of the Space Force since its establishment in 2019. Along with Space Forces Special Operations, or SPACEFOR-SOC, the service has component field commands within U.S. Northern Command, Southern Command, Pacific Command, Space Command, and Central Command. It also has a combined component for European Command and Africa Command, and sub-unified components in Japan and Korea.

As the Space Force looks to more than double its number of uniformed Guardians over the next five years—increasing its ranks from about 11,000 to 25,000 by fiscal 2031—officials have said the size of its component organizations must increase to meet operational demand.

“As we walked forward and stood up U.S. Space Force components—now with almost every combatant command around the planet—each one of those was sized to get off the ground and start doing the integrated work that we’ve seen,” Lt. Gen. Dennis Bythewood, commander of U.S. Space Forces-Space, the service’s SPACECOM component, told reporters in March. “But we already see that in stressing times, we’re having to surge people forward.”

To support future surge needs, Bythewood said at the time, components must grow to make sure that Guardian deployments don’t disrupt regular operations. He noted that his component has growth plans “already laid in” over the next few years.

The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.

The Sun has an intense and restless magnetic field. This field not only governs the star itself but is also dragged outwards along field lines by the solar wind, a stream of hot charged particles (plasma) that continuously pours out from the Sun into space. These lines can twist, snap, or fold back on themselves on their journey through the Solar System. Together, the solar wind and its dynamic field lines create all kinds of exciting activity that we can study to understand what’s happening on and around our star.

Back in 2022, ESA reported that Solar Orbiter had spotted a kink in the solar wind’s magnetic field known as a ‘switchback’. While switchbacks have been spotted often near the Sun, scientists are still debating how they form. By watching from afar, Solar Orbiter helped solve a piece of this puzzle, confirming the switchback to be S-shaped: something scientists had predicted but not seen directly.

The spacecraft has now added another crucial piece to this puzzle by tracing a switchback back to its source at the Sun. “Solar Orbiter flew through a very large switchback,” says Jesse Coburn of CNRS/LPP, France, lead author of the new paper. “Because of this, we were able to sample rarely observed particles there that have tell-tale fingerprints of their origin.”

To make this connection, Jesse and colleagues used Solar Orbiter’s Solar Wind Analyser instrument (SWA) to sample the plasma making up the switchback. At the time, Solar Orbiter was roughly halfway between Earth and the Sun.
They found a mix of charged oxygen and carbon particles that could only have formed in one way: within hot magnetic field loops at the surface of the Sun.

“There are two main competing theories for how a switchback, and by extension the solar wind, forms,” adds Jesse. “The specific mix of particles detected by Solar Orbiter is the smoking gun for a formation process known as 'interchange reconnection’.”

This kind of reconnection takes place when parts of the Sun with different magnetic properties interact. In the Sun’s atmosphere, open regions have field lines that stretch away like highways, allowing material to zoom along them into space. Closed regions have lines that initially extend into space before curving back to the Sun, creating closed loops. When an open region engages with a closed one, the lines can crowd together, snap open, and reconnect in different ways, allowing plasma that was previously trapped in a loop to escape to space.

This is what happened with this switchback – but that’s not all. The alternative theory of switchback formation involves processes related to waves and turbulence (the kind of waves that Solar Orbiter has found to play a key role in heating and accelerating the solar wind).

“Excitingly, we also see signs of these, but likely only after the switchback heads out into space,” says co-author Stephanie Yardley of Northumbria University, UK. “Once the switchback has left the Sun, waves and turbulence take over and govern how it moves.

“Overall, it seems that both processes – interchange reconnection and waves and turbulence – are involved in how switchbacks form and move through space. Our finding reconciles the two, showing that they simply operate at different stages in a switchback’s lifetime.”

To make the discovery, the researchers studied in situ observations of the switchback’s particles from Solar Orbiter’s SWA, analysed images of the Sun’s disc, and modelled the magnetic fields of both the Sun and surrounding space. They created a new model to identify where the plasma came from; this model connected the measurements from Solar Orbiter to data from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory to reveal the switchback’s solar source in unprecedented detail.

Looking beyond switchbacks, the finding reveals how the Sun heats its atmosphere and accelerates solar wind particles into space. Furthermore, it shows that the Sun’s atmosphere imprints its signature onto the particles making up this wind, giving us a possible way to read the history of solar plasma even far from the Sun.

“As humans on Earth – and in space – our lives are entangled with what’s happening on our star. The solar wind ties the Earth to the Sun, and our understanding of its dynamics has key implications for how we keep our planet safe from extreme space weather events,” says Daniel Müller, ESA Project Scientist for Solar Orbiter. “The more we know, the better we can prepare for solar storms to protect our space-based infrastructure and technology.”

“This discovery just wouldn’t have been possible without Solar Orbiter – no other spacecraft has both the proximity to the Sun and the right instruments needed to make this connection. It’s a great example of the mission delivering exactly the kind of science we knew it could, connecting the Sun to its wider environment and revealing more detail about our star.”
‘On the Coronal Origin of Magnetic Switchbacks in the Solar Wind’ by Jesse T. Coburn et al. is published today in Nature Astronomy. DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02928-0

Under the soft glow of sunrise Tuesday morning, SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket roared away from pad 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 6:33 a.m. EDT (1033 UTC) to begin a cargo run to the International Space Station.

The 35th Commercial Resupply Services (CRS-35) is carrying more than 6,300 pounds of science and supplies to the orbiting outpost when it docks to the space-facing port of the Harmony module on Thursday morning.

Fewer than 7.5 minutes after leaving the launch pad, the first stage booster, tail number B1096, wrapped up its eighth trip to space and back with a landing at Landing Zone 40 adjacent to the pad. A thunderous sonic boom rang across the spaceport and beyond, signaling its return.

Two minutes later, the Cargo Dragon spacecraft, tail number C211, separated from the Falcon 9 rocket’s upper stage to begin a two-day journey to the space station. Onboard cameras showed views of two Roll-Out Solar Array (ROSA) wings, nestled inside Dragon’s unpressurized trunk, that will be installed to augment the power of the ISS.

Built by Redwire Space, these were the fourth and final pair of ROSAs bound for the space station. Each are capable of providing more than 20 kW of power for more than 10 years. NASA has been preparing for their installation with a series of spacewalks.

“It’s been quite the journey. Folks may remember back in 2017 when we launched the ROSA on CRS-11 and that’s really where we demonstrated this innovative approach to deploying a solar array,” said Gaurang Patel, NASA’s operations integration manager of its Low Earth Orbit Program, during post-launch remarks on the agency’s broadcast.

“Once we were able to prove that technology, we were trying to understand how we could leverage this for the ISS and apply that. The legacy arrays are not outfitted to have standard upgrades and so, teams had to go look at ways we could attach these arrays. And there were non-standard interfaces where we had to put these modification kits, to safely mount these arrays.”
A version of the ROSA will be used to help power NASA’s Space Reactor 1 Freedom (SR-1 Freedom) when it launches in 2028.

Also onboard the Dragon spacecraft is the equipment necessary to support more than 40 different scientific studies. That includes a range of biological and plant science experiments as well as testing a new type of glass.

“Most ordinary glass forms from silica, the main component in sand. Unconventional glass is made from heavier elements that aren’t traditionally used to form glass. These unconventional glasses could have remarkable properties, including refractive indices higher than diamond, greater resistance to breaking, and even the ability to contract rather than expand when heated,” said Dr. Liz Warren, NASA’s deputy chief scientist within its ISS Office, during a prelaunch press conference.

“New types of glass like these could advance optics and electronics on Earth and supports space exploration with stronger, lighter, radiation-resistant, or higher-performing glass. This could potentially be used in lunar rovers and lunar habitats.”

Dragon C211 will spend about a month docked to the International Space Station. NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk will monitor the spacecraft’s arrival on Thursday.

A commercial lander that will be at the forefront of NASA’s efforts to establish a Moon Base, humanity’s first lunar outpost, has passed a series of critical tests at the agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. The tests simulated the extreme temperatures and vacuum of space, as well as the intense shaking and ear-splitting roar of launch. Results show that Voyager Technologies’ Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) spacecraft is ready to survive the rigors of space exploration.

As part of NASA’s CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative within the Moon Base Program, Griffin-1 is expected to launch later this year aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. It will deliver more than 1,100 pounds (455 kilograms) of cargo to Nobile Crater near the lunar South Pole, which categorizes it as an infrastructure-class lander. Griffin-1 will carry 10 science and technology demonstrations from six countries, including the largest commercial payload ever delivered to the Moon, Astrolab’s FLIP (FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform) rover.

“NASA JPL’s Environmental Test Laboratory has been putting robotic explorers to the test since the Ranger program gave us NASA’s first up-close views of the Moon’s surface in the mid-1960s. We’re proud to provide our expertise and facilities to support this new phase of commercial lunar exploration,” said Charles Whetsel, manager, Exploration Systems Development Office at JPL.

Testing began in July after the 2,789-pound (1,265-kilogram) spacecraft took a cross-country road trip from Voyager Lunar Systems’ manufacturing facilities in Pittsburgh to JPL in the San Gabriel Mountain foothills. Engineers spun the spacecraft on a special table to measure its mass properties, a test that enables them to look for any unexpected wobbles as they assess how the lander will move through space. Data gathered in mass properties testing is key to understanding the spacecraft’s readiness for navigation in flight and landing on the lunar surface.

To make sure signals from the spacecraft’s electronic components don’t interfere with one another, Griffin-1 underwent electromagnetic interference and electromagnetic compatibility testing inside what’s called an anechoic chamber, in which long foam spikes line the walls to absorb sound and electromagnetic waves.

During vibration testing, hundreds of sensors monitored Griffin-1 as a “shaker table” rattled it in three directions, with increasingly intense force, to simulate the ride out of Earth’s atmosphere on a massive rocket. To mimic the roar of launch, giant horns, powered by compressed nitrogen gas, blasted the spacecraft with up to 153 decibels inside a sealed acoustic chamber.

Environmental testing took place in several clean-room facilities at JPL, culminating in the 25-Foot Space Simulator, a thermal vacuum chamber listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its role in supporting historic missions like those of the Ranger, Surveyor, Mariner, and Voyager programs. Dozens of other missions (along with plenty of upgrades to the testing facility) have followed over the decades, including the Perseverance Mars rover and Europa Clipper.

Beneath the thermal vacuum chamber’s soaring 85-foot (26-meter) ceiling, for about two weeks, Griffin-1 alternately baked at up to 167 degrees Fahrenheit (75 degrees Celsius) and froze at temperatures as low as minus 148 F (minus 100 C). This testing simulates the temperature extremes the lander will experience during its journey through the vacuum of space and its operations on the lunar surface.

“Griffin-1 is being built for a historic purpose: to deliver the infrastructure and capabilities to the Moon. Seeing the spacecraft complete this demanding environmental testing is a major milestone because it demonstrates that Griffin-1 is ready for the extreme journey ahead: launch, through deep space, to the lunar South Pole,” said John Thornton, executive vice president, Voyager. “This spacecraft represents a new era of commercial lunar exploration, where missions like Griffin-1 are laying the groundwork for the Moon Base and helping turn sustained lunar exploration from a vision into a reality.”
After proving its mettle at JPL, Griffin-1 has returned to Voyager Lunar Systems’ facility for final assembly. Next up: launch-readiness operations before shipment to Cape Canaveral.

NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21.

In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA’s engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency’s programs and projects. With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.

“Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the Moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role. I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.”

“Katherine has been an extraordinary leader throughout her career, bringing technical expertise, sound judgment, and an unwavering commitment to mission success to some of NASA’s most complex engineering challenges,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer. “Her leadership has strengthened our engineering community and helped guide the agency through critical milestones and transitions. Christina brings a unique combination of engineering expertise, operational experience, and proven leadership, both on the ground and in space. I am grateful to Katherine for her exceptional service and confident Christina will continue the tradition of technical excellence that is essential to everything we do at NASA.”

Koch most recently served as a mission specialist aboard NASA’s Artemis II mission in April, helping carry out the first crewed flight around the Moon in more than 50 years. She previously spent 328 consecutive days aboard the International Space Station, setting the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman and participating in the first all-female spacewalks.

Koch began her NASA career as an electrical engineer at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, developing scientific instruments for space missions. Before her selection as an astronaut in 2013, her experience also included scientific field engineering in Antarctica and the Arctic. She has since held leadership positions within NASA’s Astronaut Office and at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, bringing a combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and firsthand understanding of the demands of human spaceflight to her new role.

Van Hooser joined NASA in 1991 at the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, beginning a distinguished career in propulsion engineering and technical leadership. Her early work focused on liquid rocket engine turbomachinery before she became chief engineer for the space shuttle main engine, leading engineering efforts through the final 21 shuttle flights. She later served as the first chief engineer for the Space Launch System’s Liquid Engines Element, helping advance the propulsion systems supporting NASA’s Artemis missions.

As Marshall’s chief engineer and, since 2023, NASA’s deputy chief engineer, Van Hooser provided critical technical leadership and oversight across the agency’s programs. Her steady guidance through complex engineering challenges and organizational transitions helped maintain continuity, strengthen collaboration, and keep mission readiness at the forefront of NASA’s work.
