William came to me for a third opinion. He was 53 and healthy, with a wife and two teenage children, a busy job, and a typically hectic work-and-family schedule. He’d taken time to do the right thing and had visited his primary care provider for a routine health exam and blood tests, his first in many years. A few weeks later, he’d found himself in an unfamiliar urologist’s office, at the edge of an abyss, ears ringing with what may be three of the most dreaded words in medicine: ‘You have cancer.’ This diagnosis portends pain, suffering and death: in the United States alone, cancer kills more than 600,000 people a year, enough lives to empty a city.

Yet, receiving a cancer diagnosis doesn’t necessarily mean what it once did. William was in very broad company: more than 2 million Americans a year receive the diagnosis and, for many, the finding entails little to no threat to length or quality of life, except through the ill effects of treatments. However, patients labelled with the ‘C-word’ face substantial clinical, psychological, social and economic consequences. This disconnect – between what the word evokes in my exam room and what it often describes in contemporary practice – drives controversies and variability in screening practices, and in light of our growing understanding of cellular biology, demands that we rethink what we really mean when we apply the label ‘cancer’.

William’s cancer was in his prostate, an organ of whose existence he was previously only vaguely aware, but whose removal or radiation risked impairments to urinary, bowel and sexual function. His biopsy had revealed a prostate tumour we designate ‘grade group 1’, which features few molecular hallmarks of cancer and no immediate potential for metastasis or death. Nonetheless, beset with many competing opinions from his rapidly expanding medical team, William found himself rushing headlong toward treatment, and wrestling with a constant anxiety he’d never felt before. By the time he reached my office, he had taken medical leave from work and confided that, perversely, he was smoking for the first time in decades.

When I started medical school in the 1990s, I found cancer fascinating and terrifying exactly because of the betrayal it represented. Most human disease represents failure of one body system or another. Whether due to trauma, infection, degradation of blood supply, mechanical wear-and-tear or other causes, one or more organs stop performing optimally. In such cases, our job in medicine is simple in principle: support the failing system, prevent further damage, and repair or replace missing function as much as possible.

Cancer is fundamentally different: although ultimately it also causes system failures, its origin lies in cells in a corner of a given organ thriving more than they should, growing too quickly, and eventually exploring and colonising other parts of the body. A marauding virus or bacterium is clearly a malign invader that can be understood and labelled as foreign and hostile. A cancer is a person’s own cells. They are behaving badly but are still intrinsic to the self. Chemotherapy for cancer is so much more toxic than antibiotics for bacterial infection precisely because it is harder for treatments to consistently distinguish ‘normal’ from ‘cancer’ among a body’s cells.
The noun, the proper noun with the capital letter, still looms, menacing

In my practices at the University of California, San Francisco Cancer Center and the San Francisco Veterans Affairs Medical Center, I see men in William’s situation in every clinic, every week. The better-informed among them have often already figured out that not every tumour needs treatment, but many are still reeling from the moment the word ‘cancer’ entered the room – the way the light suddenly dimmed and the air thickened – and how little they really heard during the rest of the visit. Counselling these patients is as important and nuanced a part of my job as is surgery, and the right words in the office are no less critical than the right tools in the operating room. But even as we have developed robot-assisted precision surgical systems, increasingly focused radiation delivery platforms and marvellously targeted pharmaceuticals, our language is essentially stuck in the 19th century.

Many colleagues and I try to pepper these counselling conversations with adjectives intended to reassure both patients and their loved ones: low-grade, low-risk, nonthreatening, slow-growing, indolent. We’ve grown relatively facile using these modifiers to pull patients back from the edge of the chasm, but the noun, the proper noun with the capital letter, still looms, menacing. After many years of these patient consultations – which have grown easier over time, but only to an extent – I am among a growing cadre of prostate cancer specialists and researchers who have started to challenge our colleagues to take seriously the question of whether to update our vocabulary to bring what we say back in line with what patients hear.

My professional forebears would recognise cancer at human scale quickly and with a knowing dread: the lump in the breast accompanied by another in the armpit, the yellowed eyes indicating a squeezed bile duct, the minor bleeding that wouldn’t stop because leukaemia had taken over the bone marrow. The unintended weight loss. The nagging pain. In my time, in contrast, we typically present a patient with the diagnosis over a piece of paper or text on a computer screen: a pathology report, a divination read from glass slides and rendered in ink or pixels to predict the future for a patient who today usually feels just fine. But at what point does aberrant behaviour threaten the whole body? How do we determine the thresholds cells cross from variant to abnormality to enemy? In the decades of my career since school, our appreciation of cancer’s complexity has grown more sophisticated, but we are still nowhere near being able to define the true moment a cancer begins, nor the subsequent moment it first threatens health and life.

Medical traditions stretching over thousands of years recognised visible growths with the capacity to grow, spread and kill. Hippocrates and his contemporaries in the 5th century BCE first named the karkinos – ‘the crab’ – after the visible tendrils that progressive tumours could be seen to propagate along lymphatic channels under the skin. In the ensuing millennia, progress in understanding the disease came in fits and starts, but cancers were universally detected when they were visible, palpable or symptomatic, by which point cure with surgery was successful only uncommonly. Even when survivable in the hard-to-imagine pre-anaesthesia, pre-antisepsis era, surgery couldn’t eradicate cancer that had already metastasised; as a result, cancers recurred and progressed – and were nearly always lethal.

In the centuries after the development of microscopy, modern pathology evolved to allow researchers and physicians to see the hidden face of the adversary: the minute cells devolved from their proper roles in the broader organism and hellbent on reproduction and migration. By the late 19th century, improved microscopes allowed early pathologists to categorise cancers – carcinomas – based not just on their organs of origin but also on the appearance of the cells themselves, laying the foundation for modern grading and staging.
The unintended consequence of screening has been over-diagnosis – the detection of lesions that would never threaten survival

Even throughout most of the microscopy era, however, cancers were still first detected based on clinically apparent symptoms, and the microscopic insights were gained only after biopsy or surgery for a cancer that was usually already relatively advanced. In these decades, the pathologist largely confirmed and refined a diagnosis made – or at least suspected – by a clinician. With the advent of cancer screening in the middle of the 20th century, however, everything changed. Screening, by definition, entails looking for early cancer in otherwise healthy people. The widespread availability of Pap smears for cervical cancer (1950s), mammography and colonoscopy for breast and colon cancer (1960s) and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing for prostate cancer (1990s) allowed cancers to be diagnosed early, by biopsy: years or even decades before they would cause clinical problems. Over time – and without any particular intention or formal conversation – the fundamental diagnosis of cancer shifted gradually from a clinical determination by a surgeon or oncologist to a histologic determination by a pathologist, setting the stage for the rift we face today.

These years also marked the advent of the War on Cancer, and diagnosing a cancer meant treating that cancer. By the time I started training early in the millennium, screening had already saved millions of lives worldwide. However, the unintended consequence of screening has been over-diagnosis – the detection of lesions that would never cause symptoms or threaten survival if left undiscovered. As I entered practice, it was becoming clear that overdiagnosis begets overtreatment and, even as screening saves lives, it harms many others through the side-effects, sometimes permanent and occasionally lethal, of unnecessary surgery, radiation and other treatments. Moreover, the diagnosis may also mean increased costs for life and health insurance, and remains associated with increased rates of depression and even suicide. So screening has proved highly controversial, driving vitriolic debates among healthcare researchers, particularly between generalists and specialists, and wild pendulum swings in screening recommendations and practices.

Cancer screening has evolved in concert with a revolution in molecular medicine. Our society’s massive investment in research over the past half-century has paid tremendous dividends. We now enjoy an unprecedented understanding of the process of carcinogenesis and of the spectacular complexity of the arms race happening every day – in William’s body, in mine, in yours, and in every animal’s – between the reproductive and evolutionary goals of individual cells and those of whole organisms. What we now understand about cancer’s origins, evolution and outcomes should drive a reconsideration of which individuals really need to bear the diagnosis.

The irregular clusters of cells we term ‘cancer’ based on their microscopic appearance are growing at all times in every body. To understand why the overwhelming majority of these are harmless, we need to return to the early history of life on Earth. Single-celled organisms emerged just about as soon as the planet became habitable, and for the next inconceivably long stretch of 2 billion years, these cells vied for survival and evolved innumerable strategies to outcompete – and sometimes consume – their neighbours and to adapt to new habitats. Eventually, evolutionary pressures drove some groups of cells to work closely together, until they started reproducing as multicellular organisms; these newly specialised cells could contribute specific functions to the life of the organism and, critically, could no longer survive on their own.

Nearly two centuries ago, the cell theorist Matthias Schleiden observed that ‘each cell leads a double life: an independent one, pertaining to its own development alone, and another incidental, insofar as it has become an integral part of a [whole].’ This tension between independence and cooperation underlies all multicellular life – and explains a cell’s fragile pact with the body. A human being contains trillions of cells, each built around the same inherited DNA coding. These cells communicate constantly with each other – and with trillions more nonhuman bacterial and fungal cells that also comprise a healthy body – through myriad local and distant signals, regulating each other’s behaviour and growth, cooperating to maximise the reproductive success of the whole person.

And yet, every one of these cells carries the genetic memory of its single-celled past and its ancient imperative to replicate. In fact, each is kept in line only though a bewilderingly complex set of internal genetic controls and external interactions with other cells. Even after an adult stops growing, about 1 per cent of cells – billions – wear out and need to be replaced every day through cell division, requiring production of a complete and preferably perfect copy of the DNA.
I am stuck explaining cancer as we now understand it biologically to patients who still understand it culturally

Our DNA is continuously assaulted by radiation; environmental pollution; and inflammation driven by unhealthy diets, smoking, chronic stress and other factors. Furthermore, every time a cell divides, thousands of copying mistakes occur. Proofreading mechanisms correct the vast majority of these, yet errors do slip through. This imperfection is critical for a whole species, for without some rate of mutation, evolution would not be possible. For an individual, on the other hand, mistakes can be deadly. A relatively small number of uncorrected mutations can send a cell hurtling toward unfettered growth. This happens daily, in every animal.

The body monitors for such rogues; early identification and eradication of genetic uprisings is a fundamental job of William’s immune system. The arms race unfolds in every hour of every day: individual cells in some part of the body start to grow too quickly or in the wrong pattern, and immune cells identify and kill them. The odds are stacked against any one aberrant cell, but over the course of years, among billions of false starts, some mutations evade detection, take hold, and propagate. Most of these early events, however, do not define a clinically meaningful cancer in that they have no ability to cause symptoms or to spread.

Over time, some tumours acquire mutations that allow cellular growth to accelerate and others that impair error-checking. With enough regulatory signals removed, cells return to their primordial imperative to reproduce and spread. Evolution at micro-scale will favour those that can propagate fastest and travel farthest, no matter the cost to the organism as a whole. For breast gland cells, for example – whose one job is to sit in place and produce milk – to migrate into lymphatic and blood channels and thrive in the unfamiliar environments of bones or lungs requires many changes to their originally programmed behaviour. All along the way, the immune system will continue to contain, if not eradicate, incipient tumours. Only those rare exceptions that learn to grow indefinitely, travel and evade the immune system threaten the organism; these are the lesions that merit the historical and cultural terror carried by the word cancer.

Yet the huge scientific progress we have made has not translated in the public vernacular. As a physician, I am stuck explaining cancer as we now understand it biologically to patients who still understand it culturally. Biologic explication cannot fully supplant historical resonance, and translation goes only so far.

The process of carcinogenesis represents a molecular continuum. Cells acquire their first mutations without any visible changes under the microscope. Eventually, enough changes accumulate that a microscopically visible neoplasm (‘new growth’) emerges and, at some point after that, the neoplasm might acquire the capacity for metastasis. In some types of cancer, this happens frequently and very quickly; in others, it happens slowly, if at all. Critically, the appearance of a symptomatic or otherwise clinically detectable tumour may happen before or after the first cells metastasise – which is the reason screening is critical to identify potentially lethal cancers within the window of opportunity for cure.

William’s decision to undergo screening for prostate cancer, setting off the cascade that landed him in my office, is a perfect example. By the time a prostate cancer causes symptoms, it is nearly always too late to cure it, and dying of prostate cancer is both painful and protracted. Therefore, when PSA – a noninvasive blood test – hit the market in the 1990s, it was widely adopted. Diagnosis rates skyrocketed for prostate cancer, which for years has been by far the most common cancer diagnosed among men in the US and other countries. Many otherwise lethal cancers were found and cured, and prostate cancer mortality rates fell by half.
These findings are so common that the term ‘incidentaloma’ has joined the clinical vernacular

By the time of my residency training, however, there was little question that, for every death prevented through surgery and radiation, multiple non-threatening cases like William’s were detected through biopsy and were still treated aggressively. Of the many men thus overtreated, far too many suffered long-term side-effects. In part because of this problem of overdiagnosis, in 2012 the US Preventive Services Task Force recommended against any routine PSA-based screening. This recommendation had the intended effect of reducing prostate cancer overdiagnosis, but also drove an increase in mortality rates, particularly for Black men, reversing a 20-year decline. I met medical students who had been taught that PSA was the paragon of a bad screening test, and I began to see more men with incurable tumours who had never been offered one – or worse, had been refused a test even when they’d asked for it.

Grade group 1 prostate cancer – the lowest-grade form, with no immediate potential to spread or cause death – is exceedingly common. Among men who die in their 70s or 80s of non-cancer causes, these cells are found on autopsy in about half; among men in their 30s, the figure is about 20 per cent. They are not clinically meaningful cancers and may be better understood as a feature of normal male ageing. William’s low-grade prostate cancer was detected because he underwent an appropriate mid-life PSA screening, but it had likely been present for years before and was still many years away from threatening his life.

In addition to the many cancers detected through explicit screening, another large proportion are detected today more or less accidentally. I may order a CT scan for a patient with pain suggestive of a kidney stone, only to find that in addition to the stone there is an abnormality in the kidney, liver, pancreas or some other organ. These findings are so common that the originally tongue-in-cheek term ‘incidentaloma’ has worked its way into the clinical vernacular. Finding such lesions is occasionally fortuitous. I once took care of a young patient whose life was saved by an amoebic infection he picked up while travelling in South Asia; had he not been imaged for unrelenting abdominal pain, we likely would not have discovered his large, high-grade kidney cancer before it was too late. Much more often, however, we find and aggressively treat small lesions that would never have caused any problem if left undiagnosed, no matter their appearance under the microscope.

Public screening debates have grown bitter and tribal because both sides believe they are protecting patients from different versions of catastrophe. The surgeon, the oncologist and the advanced cancer patient see the metastases, the pain, the missed window, the death. The primary care physician or public policymaker sees the complications of treatment, the permanent declines in quality of life, the needless anxiety, and the costs. Both are reacting to real suffering, but the latter narratives more easily diffuse into intangible statistics, whereas the former resonate more powerfully and feel less forgivable. One patient asks: ‘Why did you talk me into the radiation that has left me with permanent bowel problems?’ while the other demands: ‘Why didn’t you order a simple test that could have saved me years of pain and let me watch my grandkids grow up?’

I regularly see both situations: patients suffering devastating side-effects of treatment they never needed, and others with incurable cancers that could have been found much earlier – some of whom had even asked for a screening test and were refused. My reservations about overdiagnosis and overtreatment have not made me a screening sceptic, but a screening test today should be only the first step on a possible journey to a diagnosis. William’s slightly elevated PSA should have prompted one of a dozen blood, urine or imaging tests designed to predict the presence or absence of potentially lethal prostate cancer. A negative test implies either a normal prostate or a grade group 1 cancer, and in either case we forego the biopsy – telling the patient more or less explicitly that if there is only low-grade disease present, both we and he are perfectly happy not knowing about it.
For the latter, the right path is active surveillance – deferring treatments and following carefully with every expectation of cure if there are signs of progression.

This paradigm was pioneered at my centre and a few others nearly 30 years ago, but has only recently gained traction in community practice, and implementation is still highly variable. In the US, too many financial, legal and cultural factors favour treatment over observation, a somewhat embarrassing reality to acknowledge in counselling visits.
We neither need nor want to know about every over-eager cell with the desire to grow but without the toolkit to travel

By the time William had his first visit with me, he had already been booked for surgery at one hospital and strongly pushed toward radiation at another. Many patients I meet in exactly this situation simply cannot get past the word, the diagnosis; they cannot reconcile with the idea that I would not want to treat what they see as a life-threatening diagnosis. Despite my best efforts at reassurance, none of my adjectives can tame the noun ‘cancer’, and too many patients wind up finding another doctor to offer unnecessary treatment.

Other examples abound. Basal cell carcinomas of the skin are so pervasive that cancer registries do not even track them. They can almost always be cured by simple excision. If neglected, they can grow quite large and can be disfiguring, but almost never spread, despite the carcinoma label.

Ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast by definition does not invade, and recent trials have suggested at least some such lesions can be monitored much like low-grade prostate cancer. In the case of thyroid cancer, pathologists have already crossed this bridge. A subset of lesions once classified as thyroid carcinoma were renamed ‘noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features’ – mercifully abbreviated to NIFTP – because they don’t justify the full weight of ‘carcinoma’. Likewise, some small, low-grade bladder lesions once called cancer are now labelled ‘papillary urothelial neoplasms of low malignant potential’.

At the same time, we may be careening toward a new, fraught era of accelerated overdetection. All screening efforts to date have emerged from organ system-specific tests. Now, commercially available whole-body MRI scans marketed to the ‘worried well’ – and well-off – will surely multiply the number of incidentalomas we find every year. In parallel, so-called multi-cancer early detection tests promise to reveal molecular signals – fragments of DNA – of many cancers from a single blood draw. If they work well, they may save lives. But they also raise the stakes for the question that screening has already raised: when detection moves backward along the cancer journey from palpable lump, to abnormal cells, to molecular harbingers, what exactly are we naming? We neither need nor want to know about every slightly over-eager cell with the molecular desire to grow but without the genetic toolkit required to travel.

If the borders around ‘cancer’ are blurry, the boundaries of ‘normal’ are too. Normal-appearing cells often feature many cancer-typical mutations. Biology operates across bell curves, and clinical risk follows suit. In short, we don’t need to designate a given abnormality a cancer to justify treatment. We routinely remove colon polyps that may or may not presage cancer because the risks are typically negligible. In a more extreme example, some women with inherited BRCA mutations elect prophylactic mastectomy and oophorectomy – major surgery with substantial quality-of-life implications – because the spectre of possible future lethal cancer looms so darkly.

Medicine’s Greek and Latin shibboleths long served physicians better than patients. Dubbing a newly described but not-yet-understood region of the brain locus coeruleus lent an air of authority that ‘blue place’ would not have done. Today, our understanding of disease has grown along with our commitment to patient autonomy. But a very recent development in this vein, open medical records, exposes patients to language they may not understand. The result is that, all too often, the ‘you have cancer’ moment is lived only by a patient alone with a screen.

When I perform biopsies, I try to forewarn patients of the language they may see on the pathology report before we talk again, but there are limits to how much I can explain in advance. This problem is all the worse because we cancer specialists inhabit a borderland our vocabulary has not yet evolved to govern. The binary language of ‘normal’ vs ‘cancer’ suited the long epoch in which disease announced itself clinically but is badly strained in an era in which screening tests and incidental scans identify biological possibility long before clinical destiny. Pathologists describe what they see through the microscope, but a diagnosis is more than a description. When a word rises off a pathology report, whether into my exam room or the patient’s living room, it becomes prognosis, identity, fear, crisis.

Screening offers a transformative opportunity but can be implemented safely across populations only if we can distinguish and name ‘real’ cancers – those with the ability to spread and kill – as separate from the pretenders. Researchers and oncologists alike often speak of distinguishing ‘kittens’ from ‘lions’. Some kittens may evolve into lions, but these are the minority and can usually be identified before the lion escapes the enclosure.
We shouldn’t embark on a needless civil war against these minor malcontents

Modern medicine loves classification yet falls oddly short in oncology. Our international system for diagnostic coding recognises 18 codes in the heading of ‘contact with other nonvenomous reptiles’ yet only a single code for the huge spectrum of biology that is prostate cancer, regardless of aggressiveness or clinical relevance. If we’re not careful naming the boundary between abnormality and disease, then we risk wounding our patients with the name ‘cancer’ itself.

In 2026, then, should my colleagues really have handed William a cancer diagnosis? Am I required to validate that diagnosis when everything we have learned over a quarter-century screams otherwise? Increasingly, we can tell the lions from the kittens. But after thousands of years, the karkinos still looms large in cultural memory, and the term ‘carcinoma’ on a pathology report still connotes pain, loss and death. I still meet patients who book appointments specifically to set up surgery and look at me with incredulity at the suggestion that that would be the wrong first step.

Perhaps it is high time for the medical community to reconsider how we define cancer, and to bring the diagnosis back into line with enduring public perception. Cancer, in the sense that has always haunted the public imagination, spreads and kills. Precursor lesions – molecular or pathological – are not ‘normal’, but we have no shortage of alternative vocabulary with which to label them, as well as the tools to safely follow them. Most will never amount to any meaningful insurgency, and we shouldn’t embark on a needless civil war against these minor malcontents. If we permanently address overdiagnosis by simply declining to diagnose low-grade lesions, we can screen much more broadly and with greater confidence. Such a change would improve trust between patients and their doctors, and between primary care providers and their consulting specialists. Relabelling would also very likely save thousands of lives.

William needs attention to his prostate no matter what labels we hang on it. He needs my counselling and monitoring. Someday, I may need to guide him toward treatment. But what he did not need, on the day he walked into my office having already rearranged his life around a word, was to live in the full shadow of a disease that was not yet threatening him. Revising the label would not only reduce overtreatment but would also finally realign our language with our science, with our systems of classification and with patients’ lived reality. Cancer is a cellular rebellion that spreads and kills. The rest of the microscopic borderland deserves a different, gentler name.

Christopher Nolan’s epic The Odyssey is coming home, and fortunately for movie fans, it didn’t take ten years. The film will hit video-on-demand platforms and get a Blu-ray release on Nov. 17, exactly four months after its U.S. theatrical release.

The release was first announced in August, but we now have more details about what’s for sale. In addition to the 4K, Blu-ray, and DVD releases, the film will be released as a collectible Steelbook and a collectible $300 three-disc set. Both the collectible set and the Steelbook have sold out since landing online. It will also be able to buy or rent on digital the same day.
No streaming date has been announced, although as a Universal Pictures release, it is expected to eventually land on Peacock.

Based on Homer’s 2,700-year-old epic poem of the same name, The Odyssey follows Odysseus (Matt Damon) as he tries to return home to Ithaca after fighting in the Trojan War. In true Nolan fashion, the film bounces around the timeline rather than following a straightforward narrative. In addition to Damon, the film stars Tom Holland, Zendaya, Robert Pattinson, and Lupita Nyong’o.

The Odyssey raised the already high box office bar set by Nolan’s previous movies, raking in over $1.7 billion worldwide against a $250 million budget, according to Box Office Mojo. A significant chunk of that revenue came from IMAX screens, the premium large-scale format that The Odyssey was filmed for.

“Once you’ve stepped into this film and let it sweep you up, however, it’s hard to deny the accomplishment that he’s brought to the screen,” wrote Rolling Stone’s David Fear of the film. “You may have no idea how long you’ve been gone after you’ve seen it. You just know that you want to go back again.”

When a filmmaker tells a story based on real events, especially ones that are inspiring or heroic, there’s always a risk of hagiography. “Clean Hands” is a movie where the storytellers either take a lot of license with an actual person’s life to add drama, or don’t seem aware just how unflattering their subject’s behavior actually is. Written, produced and directed by Jake Allyn (“Ride”), the film chronicles the relationship between real-life Hagerstown, MD narcotics officer Kevin Simmers (Zach Braff) and his efforts to rescue his daughter Brooke (Esther McGregor) from the grip of drug abuse. But while the “happening right under his nose” details lend a heartbreaking edge to a sadly familiar story, the script’s argument against criminalizing addiction reconciles uneasily with its portrayal of Simmers’ determination to save Brooke by any means necessary.

Simmers is a hero cop, looked up to by his colleagues and liked better than one might expect by the local townspeople, given his by-the-book approach. Though he maintains a close relationship with 19-year-old Brooke, he’s blindsided when he learns that she’s addicted to Percocet and has been consorting with abusive dealer Brick (Kraig Dane). After unsuccessfully trying to enroll her in a private rehab facility, Simmers learns that she’s moved on to heroin; he takes a tough-love approach to let her get arrested, hoping to scare her straight. But when even that fails, he becomes determined to cut off her supply at the source, pursuing local addicts in the hopes of apprehending anyone who might deal her drugs.

Despite the support of his religious wife Dana (Abigail Spencer) and colleagues on the police force, including an ambitious deputy (Lucas Till) eager to succeed him as the precinct’s role model, Simmers’ efforts to help get Brooke clean fail over and over again. As he faces the prospect of losing her to addiction, he begins to conceive an alternative path for struggling drug abusers, even while witnessing members of the Hagerstown community — including some of his fellow officers — exploiting addicts instead of helping them.

Given the infomercial pasted at the top of the closing credits for Brooke’s House, the rehab facility Simmers created in response to his daughter’s addiction, it feels safe to assume that the former police officer fully endorsed this portrait of him and his family’s struggles. Yet the typical disclaimer absolving the filmmakers of responsibility for dramatizing these real people’s lives is oddly posted at the beginning of the closing credits rather than at the very end, suggesting that some of the narrative leaps taken here by the filmmakers are bigger than usual. To that end, one can understand why Allyn wouldn’t want to risk misrepresenting Hagerstown law enforcement. But should audiences accept at face value every action taken by Simmers in his crusade to save his daughter?

By all accounts, he was a dedicated cop with honed instincts as an investigator, and a loving father to Brooke — so much so that, in the film, Dana accuses the two of them of being addicted to each other. But the character’s compassion towards perpetrators and his cool detachment under pressure seem only to apply when he doesn’t have an active stake in a crime. When he does, he seems willing to abuse his power and take any measures that he thinks will result in whatever he’s already decided the outcome should be — whether that’s lying to a healthcare provider to get his daughter treatment, or arresting an individual he deems complicit in Brooke’s condition.

As the film tells it, Simmers eventually learns that waging war against dealers and community enablers makes less of an impact on people who are addicted than providing them consistent, patient, loving support. But the character is so relentless for so long with his methods that it’s hard not to pin a portion of the blame for Brooke’s addiction on him.

Again, that seems distantly like the point (or at least one point) of “Clean Hands.” But Allyn is entirely too interested in Simmers’ police work, meaning high-pitched chases and strong-arm interrogations, to strike the right balance between his day job and his earnest efforts to help his daughter. As a viewer, it’s possible to forgive a character who’s so determined to protect his daughter that he takes overbearing or inappropriate measures, but when the film wants the crime stuff to be tense and exciting — amplified with music by instrumental rock act Those Who Ride With Giants — it undercuts the humanity of what that character is facing.

Simmers marks a departure from the kinds of roles for which Braff is best known, and the actor commits to the character’s tenacity and determination in a way that suggests he’s either prioritizing authenticity regardless of how the character is perceived, or he misunderstands how sympathetic Allyn’s version of Simmers can be. The problem is the contrast between his well-meaning actions and their impact on others: Brooke faces beatings in jail because her father antagonizes the guards and other inmates, God-fearing Dana flinches every time he drops an f-bomb or angrily dresses down a rehab administrator, and until the very last scene in the film, he ignores or dismisses the addiction, poverty or desperation of anyone he encounters who’s struggling.

McGregor offers a welcome counterbalance as Brooke, whose general disposition emanates from her relationship with her father, even as it’s hobbled by troubles the script pinpoints with delicacy. Though the film doesn’t quite know what to do with Dana as Simmers bulldozes his way to a cure for Brooke, Spencer similarly offers grace — or at least a less rigid form of support — that hints at how his initial way of helping may not be the most effective one.

To whatever extent this story is told accurately, Simmers was of course doing the best that he could to reckon with a challenge he’d dealt with in the line of duty, but never with a person so close to him — and years of repetition reinforced a one-size-fits-all reaction to an affliction that must be addressed individually. But the film builds to the founding of Brooke’s House and its immediate, overwhelming success, indicating that all Simmers needed to do was change his tactics, instead of the more meaningful, moving change in his perception of addiction as something to be mechanically repaired. A handful of appealing performances aside, “Clean Hands” ignores too many messy realities in favor of quick solutions; the stuff that gives a true story like this power is the hard work and struggle that happens between an epiphany about oneself and the reality of implementing its lessons in the world.
DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
Scientists have recorded how a single fertilized egg becomes a complex body, uncovering hidden patterns of development that could shed light on birth defects and cancer.
- University of Washington School of Medicine/UW Medicine

- Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

Scientists have reconstructed a remarkably detailed family tree of cells in a developing mouse embryo, tracing their origins back to the moment a fertilized egg first divided into two cells. Using an innovative DNA recording technology, the researchers followed how those early cells multiplied, developed specialized roles, and eventually helped form a body with distinct organs and tissues.
The recording covered the first 13.5 days of embryonic development, providing an unusually detailed look at how a complex mammalian body takes shape. (Full gestation in mice is 19 to 21 days.)
The findings, published on October 8, 2026, in the journal Science, could help scientists better understand normal development and what happens when that process goes wrong.

"We are interested in tracking how cells' early ancestry in an embryo influences their later fates. Exploring cell lineages helps decode normal development. Such research could eventually advance knowledge about congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental conditions, genetic disorders or cancer," said Dr. Jay Shendure, a professor of genome sciences at the University of Washington School of Medicine in Seattle and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator.
Shendure led the research alongside Dr. Chengxiang Qiu, a molecular and systems biologist at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. Both served as senior authors of the study.
A DNA Typewriter Records the History of Living Cells
The achievement was made possible by a technology called DNA Typewriter, developed by Shendure and Junhong Choi, who is now at Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
Rather than simply observing cells as they divide, the system allows scientists to preserve a record of their history directly within their DNA.

To accomplish this, the researchers inserted a redesigned recording sequence, which they call a tape, into the genome of a fertilized mouse egg. The updated design made it easier to recover the information stored in individual cells.

As the embryo developed, the DNA Typewriter remained embedded in the genetic material of its cells, recording their divisions in a way that could later be used to reconstruct their ancestry. The result was something like a biological logbook, documenting the sequence of events that gave rise to different cell populations.

"Think of it like an actual typewriter, except it types onto a cell's own DNA instead of paper," explained Haedong Kim, a co-first author of the study and a postdoctoral scientist in genome sciences at UW Medicine, the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. "Every time a cell divides, it strikes one new character onto the next blank line -- always in order, never overwriting what's already there. Because the characters are always filled in sequence, that sequence itself spells out the cell's division history."

Because these markings are passed down to daughter cells, researchers can examine the recorded sequences and identify which cells descended from a shared ancestor. Cells carrying matching portions of the record can be linked together, allowing scientists to reconstruct branches of the embryo's family tree.
"Writing the record is only half the problem. You also have to read it back out of each cell, so we redesigned the tape to make that easier," said Kim.
Overcoming a Major Challenge in Developmental Biology

Reconstructing the entire history of a developing mammal has long been a formidable challenge. As an embryo grows, its cells divide repeatedly and begin taking on specialized functions. Following those relationships becomes increasingly difficult as the number and variety of cells expand.
Scientists accomplished a similar feat decades ago in a tiny roundworm, but that animal has a relatively simple body with far fewer cells. Its transparency also makes development easier to study.

Mammals are considerably more complicated. Earlier technologies provided important insights into mouse embryonic development, but they generally captured only portions of the larger cellular family tree.

Some traditional recording techniques also have significant limitations. They work by cutting DNA to create identifying marks, which can damage cells and erase information left by earlier divisions. Their recording capacity is limited, and because the marks are not necessarily created in a fixed sequence, scientists must attempt to reconstruct the order of events afterward.

"DNA Typewriter avoids all of this," said Kim. "It writes without fully severing the DNA, keeps recording relatively steadily, and writes everything in strict order, so we can record cell lineages at much higher resolution for a longer time."
Tracing an Embryo Back to Its First Two Cells
The researchers began by attempting to record development in 100 fertilized mouse eggs. Of those, 10 embryos were ultimately available for examination.

One specimen, identified as Embryo No. 3, stood out because its DNA recording system had functioned particularly well and preserved the most extensive developmental history. The scientists therefore concentrated their detailed analysis on that embryo.
One of the most important discoveries came from a recording made at the very beginning of development, immediately after the fertilized egg divided for the first time.

"Our recording captured a clear, permanent mark distinguishing the two very first cells, letting us trace nearly every cell we profiled from the embryo back to one or the other," said Kim. "One of these two founding cells did go on to produce more descendants than the other, but they produced diverse cell types at almost equal ratios."
This meant that although one of the original cells contributed more descendants overall, both founding cells gave rise to a remarkably similar mix of specialized cell types.
The finding illustrates how scientists can now investigate the earliest stages of development with a level of detail that was previously difficult to achieve.
Scientists Discover When Cells Choose Their Roles
The DNA recordings also revealed important information about when cells begin committing to their eventual roles in the body.

Early embryonic cells can give rise to many different types of tissue. As development progresses, their descendants gradually become more specialized, eventually forming structures such as the nervous system, skin, blood, and eyes.
By reconstructing the branches of the embryo's cellular family tree, the researchers could determine when different groups of cells began following distinct developmental paths.
Their observations were consistent with conclusions drawn from decades of previous research, but the new approach allowed them to examine these patterns within a single developing mouse.

"Blood cells and the retina committed relatively early, while the skin's outer layer didn't commit until noticeably later," the researchers explained. "Cell fate wasn't locked in all at once. Different cell types settled into their identity on their own separate schedules, some early and some late."
These findings show that the transition from a flexible, unspecialized cell to one with a particular biological function does not happen at the same time throughout the embryo.

Instead, different tissues follow their own developmental timelines. Some cells begin narrowing their possible futures early, while others remain flexible for a longer period before becoming committed to a specific role.
What This Could Mean for Birth Defects, Cancer, and Stem Cell Therapies
Understanding exactly how cells acquire their identities could eventually have important implications for medicine.

Many developmental disorders arise when the normal process of cell specialization or tissue formation is disrupted. Cancer also involves abnormal cell behavior, including failures in the mechanisms that ordinarily regulate cell growth and division.
By tracing cellular ancestry and identifying when different developmental pathways emerge, scientists may gain a clearer understanding of how these problems begin.

"This kind of large-scale developmental recording gives scientists a map of how one cell becomes a whole body -- which helps explain how organs form correctly, how that process can go wrong in birth defects, and how abnormal cell growth drives cancer. As stem cell engineering advances, this kind of recording can also help guide how we engineer cells for therapeutic use."

Although the work was conducted in mouse embryos and does not yet represent a direct medical treatment, it demonstrates a powerful way to study the biological decisions that shape a developing organism.
The approach could also support future stem cell research, particularly efforts to guide cells toward specific identities for regenerative medicine and other therapeutic applications.

Additional co-first authors included Qi Yu and Sophie Seidel, both affiliated with the University of Washington School of Medicine's Department of Genome Sciences and the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology.

Shendure serves as the lead scientific director of the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology. He is also scientific director of the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine and the Allen Institute for Cell Lineage Tracing.

Despite his ongoing struggles, Shohei Ohtani will be in the Game 3 starting lineup for the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers, manager Dave Roberts announced Tuesday.

"He's adamant he feels good enough to be in there. He's close to finding something with his swing. I feel great about it," Roberts said Tuesday. "He wants to be in there and help us win a ballgame and win a championship. Great conversation, and I'm excited about having him in there."

Ohtani, who is nursing knee and biceps injuries, is 3 for 20 this postseason and 11 for 70 (.157) with zero home runs in his last 24 games dating back to August 18. He spent 12 days on the injured list in September and has just one hit in eight NLCS plate appearances as the Dodgers have fallen behind 2-0 in the best-of-seven series.

"The results, I take full responsibility," Ohtani said through an interpreter Tuesday. "That's all I can really say, why the results haven't been where I wanted it to be. I think there's different approaches to this, whether that be focusing on reducing the symptoms and getting rid of the pain and/or just making sure that I'm moving well in the swing."

, Roberts said the Dodgers would have a "conversation" about Ohtani's place in the lineup. He is clearly not himself at the plate. His swings are off-balance and his contact quality is way down. Simply put, Ohtani looks like an injured player -- one who is not capable of helping his team score runs or win games at the moment.

"The symptoms have subdued a lot," Ohtani said. "Especially when I was on the IL, spending that time just being able to reduce the symptoms. As of now with the swing, it's a daily process of trying different things, different feel on a daily basis."

The Dodgers have a very good DH alternative in top prospect Josue De Paula. De Paula, 21, reached base 21 times in 11 regular-season games and has pinch-hit three times in key spots this postseason, and worked two walks. Los Angeles has nine singles and one double in the two NLCS losses to the Brewers. Their offense is lacking.

"We remember vividly at this time last year that he maybe had the best baseball game ever played the day he pitched against us and hit a home run every time up, it seemed like," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Wednesday when asked about Ohtani's struggles at the plate. "You can't forget that, his capabilities."

Now 32, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 30 home runs during the regular season, which would be a career year for most players but is a down year for Ohtani. He threw 85 ⅔ innings with a 1.79 ERA before the injuries. Ohtani has not pitched since July 3 and won't return to the mound this postseason.
Teams with a 2-0 lead in a best-of-seven series have historically gone on to win the series 83% of the time. Game 3 is Wednesday night at Dodger Stadium.

Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual. It’s fast-paced and unruly, depicting a family of five as they rush through the morning routine. There’s yelling and mess, misplaced keys and discarded eggshells. Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.
Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
The chaos is surprisingly real for an Apple commercial.
But the spot has parents — those with teen children in particular — feeling seen.

I’ll admit that it stressed me out the first time I watched it, too. Mornings getting my five-year-old out the door are a special breed of chaos, and usually culminate in us playing whatever ad-libbed game will get him to put his shoes on. But it’s not quite as intense as this one, which features dad making French toast, mom losing and finding keys in her pocket, a proxy battle over the thermostat, a teenage boy helping himself to whipped cream from a can, and an unexpected video call. There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch. It’s a lot for just over three minutes of screentime.

If I know anything, though, I know to trust my colleague Jen Tuohy, senior reviewer and parent to two teens, on matters of the home. Her take? “The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.”

Other parents of teens shared similar reactions on Threads. When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.

Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? I don’t believe any teenager trusts Apple’s privacy features that far.

The confusion about the commercial is understandable. This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the course of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse.

But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.

A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? These are questions worth answering before you start drilling holes in your kitchen island! In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug. Just ask a parent.

An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, who federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room.

He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing.
OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device that had not been installed in Alfozan’s bag at the office.

Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US district court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest.

Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.”

OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep.

Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview, Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations.

The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment.

Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies.
According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.”

The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated.

OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted.

After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing.

According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found.

He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

Battle lines shift in House races as Republicans retreat from front-line districts
Republicans are retreating from several key U.S. House races, while Democrats are racing to raise funds for candidates who seemed unlikely to win earlier this year

DES MOINES, Iowa -- Republicans were retreating Tuesday from a handful of battleground U.S. House races while Democrats were racing to raise money to boost candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year.

The Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading House Republican super PAC, canceled spending in four races from the Midwest to the East Coast and increased its investment in 16 other races from Texas to Pennsylvania.

Meanwhile, Democrats' House campaign committee is eyeing openings in Republican-held districts and hoping to raise millions of dollars in the next week to fuel a late round of advertising that they say could net at least a half dozen more seats.

The shifting money in the final three weeks of midterm campaigns points to an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on President Donald Trump's weak approval ratings.

“A lot of seats are in the competitive range, and only really two are — maybe three — are possible Republican pickups," said David McIntosh, president of the conservative Club For Growth, noting voter dissatisfaction with the economy and Republican dissatisfaction with Congress' inability to pass Trump's SAVE Act regarding voter registration. "It looked like Republicans were weak, and so you’ve seen a lot of drop-off in enthusiasm.”
“You can tell now where people are competing based on where they’re putting the money,” said Stu Sandler, a Republican strategist working on House and statewide races this year.

The Congressional Leadership Fund is no longer spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st District, where three-term Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks is defending her seat against Democrat Christina Bohannan, according to two Republican campaign officials familiar with the group's plans.
The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to share private strategy conversations.

Bohannan is running for her third time against Miller-Meeks. Last time, the race was decided by only 799 votes, making it the second-closest in the country. It's an eastern Iowa district where congressional cuts to Medicaid have been linked to hospital service closures and high diesel prices have been a challenge for farmers.

Likewise, the officials said the group won't keep spending in New Jersey's 7th District, where second-term Republican Rep. Tom Kean is facing off against Democrat Rebecca Bennett. Kean has been under scrutiny for his four-month absence from Congress, which he left unexplained until disclosing a mental health crisis upon his return. Kean, who won by 5.4 percentage points two years ago, has also faced questions over his support for Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war.

These races, as well as one in the Cincinnati, Ohio, area and one in east-central Michigan, have accounted for $13.3 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending, more than 12% of its total through Oct. 13.
The group is reinforcing its spending in a series of districts where Trump beat Democrat Kamala Harris by narrow margins in 2024.
Sandler said his party needs to turn out voters who usually participate in presidential elections but often stay home in the midterms.
“One thing you can’t say is that they’ve been under-resourced,” he said. “Republican resources are at a high. They’ve never been this well-funded in the midterm.”

As House Republicans have retrenched, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee believes at least a dozen more races could be within striking distance. However, they need more money to take advantage.
The committee launched a $17 million fundraising drive, with a deadline of Oct. 22, to pump advertising onto the air in districts that were once seen as out of reach.

“It’s not that we need the money to win in the districts where we have been running to get to 218 seats,” said Courtney Rice, the committee’s communication director. “We’re talking about the next level.”

One is Ohio's 10th, a Dayton-area district represented by 12-term Republican Rep. Mike Turner. Democrats see Turner as beatable despite the former Dayton mayor's durability and 18 percentage-point victory two years ago. Trump carried the district by six percentage points in 2024.

Turner didn't begin advertising until late September, according to AdImpact, later than most competitive House incumbents, and the National Republican Congressional Committee started spending there this week.

If the Democratic committee reaches its goal, it would also start spending in the Miami area, suburban St. Louis, Missouri and the Little Rock, Arkansas, area. They would be able to buy ads in coordination with the campaigns at the lower rate available to candidates, due to a June Supreme Court decision, squeezing more ad time from those dollars.

Senate Republicans are pouring millions more into Nebraska to protect Sen. Pete Ricketts, the latest sign of how dramatically their spending priorities have shifted from battleground states toward defending seats they once expected to hold comfortably.
Ricketts is facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn, who is backed by Democrats. Trump won Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024.
The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, said Tuesday it was behind a $15 million investment in the state.
Other groups are also pumping money into the race, with the cryptocurrency-backed super PAC Fairshake launching a $7 million advertising campaign, according to AdImpact data.

The group has also increased its investment in Ohio’s Senate race, bringing its total spending there to $45 million in support of Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is up against Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown.

The Nebraska investment follows new spending by the Senate Leadership Fund in Kansas and South Carolina, two other states Trump won by double digits in 2024. All three were absent from the group’s initial $342 million advertising plan in April, which has since been reshaped as Republicans pulled back from Georgia and North Carolina, two states that were central to their original strategy.

Democrats are also shifting their resources. The Senate Democrats’ main spending arm said Tuesday it was pulling its advertising last week from Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has built a substantial fundraising advantage over Republican Rep. Mike Collins, and focusing instead on Maine, New Hampshire, Michigan, Iowa, Kansas, Texas, Alaska and Ohio.

The shifting investments come as both parties make their final spending decisions in the battle for Senate control, with Democrats pointing to their candidates and the political environment as potential counterweights to Republican money.
In a letter to fellow senators Tuesday, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said the battle for control of the chamber “comes down to one defining question.”
“Will the unprecedented tsunami of Republican money defeat the massive Democratic advantage in candidates, policies, and political climate?” Schumer asked.

Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican announces after surgery
Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.

The surgery, performed at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involved removing the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung, according to a statement by Leo's doctors released by the church. Lung tissue examined after the surgery confirmed a previous test that revealed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said.
Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the most common form of lung cancer in the United States, representing about 40% of all lung cancers, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.

The Pope's surgery, which the doctors said was successful, lasted about 90 minutes, after which Leo awoke normally and, following a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the hospital's 10th floor.

At 71 years old, Leo is relatively young for a pope – and remains physically active. He works out weekly, including regular tennis matches with his personal secretary and enjoys riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat.

Leo has not been known to smoke, but there is a history of cancer in the pope's family. On Tuesday, the Vatican announced that Leo's older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, is currently hospitalized with a form of cancer. And Leo's mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990 at age 77. Back in 1984, while living in Rome, the future pope wrote to several friends saying, "my mother continues to undergo chemotherapy treatments. … She's a tough lady and handles it all well, which makes it a little easier for me being so far from Chicago."
The Vatican says the Pope has essentially cleared his public schedule for the next several days, until at least October 20. The Vatican has yet to announce any further treatments.

It’s been understood for a long time that being able to control valve lift, duration and timing is a great way to optimize various aspects of engine performance. It can enhance power, throttle response, fuel economy and emissions, and engine designers have devised hydraulic, electro-hydraulic and even “camless” systems that use poppet valves rather than a conventional valve train. With stricter emissions standards in place, many manufacturers see variable valve timing (VVT) as a good way to hit those targets.

A lumpy racing cam can introduce a lot more air into the combustion chambers, enhancing efficiency, but that usually means a rough idle and possible drivability problems at lower RPMs. A less aggressive cam might mean a smooth idle, but when intake valves close too early at higher engine speeds it can compromise performance. If both intake and exhaust valves are open, even just momentarily, it can cause unburnt fuel to exit the engine or can push unburnt gases back into the intake manifold.

Earlier VVT systems were two-step designs, with one timing profile for engine speeds below 3500 RPM or so, and another timing and lift profile for engine speeds above 3500 RPM. Newer VVTs are designed for infinite adjustment throughout the RPM range.

VVT systems date back as far as early aircraft engines and even steam locomotives, while Fiat was the first manufacturer to introduce a successful VVT design in the late ‘60s. One of the most successful and reliable systems, though, has been Honda’s Variable Valve Timing and Lift Electronic Control (VTEC) and i-VTEC designs. Honda’s systems have been around since model year 1989. Let’s take a closer look.

Any VVT system is designed to change the relationship between the crankshaft and camshaft. Older, simpler systems use a phaser that enables a range of adjustment, but only for valve timing and not lift and duration. Here’s a quick breakdown of how VTEC performs:
As RPMs go up, the engine management computer directs oil through the rocker shaft (the horizontal tube that runs through all the rocker arms).
As this oil pressure goes up, a pin is actuated and slides through the low-RPM rocker arms, locking them together with a third high-RPM rocker arm.

Each cylinder has a third lobe on the camshaft, situated between the lobes for intake and exhaust valves, and this third rocker arm follows that lobe and its profile to optimize valvetrain operation for higher engine speeds.

This technology was first explored on Honda’s motorcycle engine, then Honda’s New Engine Concept project (unveiled in 1984) helped convince the OEM’s management that a dynamic cam phasing system was a good feature for enhancing engine performance.

The i-VTEC (“i” for Intelligent) debuted in 2001 and uses an adjustable cam gear that’s actuated by oil pressure. The ECM constantly monitors engine load and RPMs to make adjustments to cam timing in real time, while the VTEC system only kicks in at about 4000 RPMs or more. i-VTEC is available in two different iterations: one for performance engines (think Civic Si or Acura TSX) and one for economy and daily drivers (think Accord or CR-V). With i-VTEC setups, the camshaft for intake valves can be adjustable from 25 to 50 degrees, from fully retarded at idle to mild advance at full throttle.

i-VTEC is still featured in select naturally-aspirated models, including the Civic, HR-V and CR-V, although it’s gradually being phased out in favor of turbocharging and more standard VTC systems. It can still be found in Honda’s K-series, R-series, J-series and L-series engine families.

In economy setups, with four valves per cylinder, VTEC-E can effectively make the engine operate as a 12-valve by shutting down one intake valve at lower RPMs. Honda’s V6 engines pair up the i-VTEC design with Variable Cylinder Management (VCM), which shuts down three or even four cylinders during light-load, steady RPM situations such as highway cruising. Honda now also offers turbo four-cyliners with i-VTEC for even more performance and power.
VTEC adds a layer of complexity to any engine, and it does sometimes come with some service bugs, despite Honda’s reputation for reliability.

- Low oil volume or dirty oil can affect operation, since VTEC relies on oil pressure to lock the rocker arms together with the more aggressive cam lobe. Low oil levels or contaminated oil can starve the system.
- Dirty oil can contaminate and clog the tiny mesh filter behind the VTEC solenoid.
- VTEC solenoids and pressure switches have been known to fail or become stuck mechanically.
- In some instances, a failed pressure switch or sensor fault can limit RPMs to about 3000, triggering limp mode and an illuminated CEL.

These problems can register trouble codes P1259/P1253 (system malfunction or circuit failure), P2646/P2647 (rockers oil pressure switch circuit low/high) or OBD1 codes 21 or 22 (VTEC solenoid valve or VTEC oil pressure switch).

If you suspect a solenoid issue, touch a 12v jumper wire to the solenoid terminal; even with the engine off, you should hear a click as the internal plunger moves. In many cases, the pickup screen for the solenoid can be cleaned of gunk and debris with Brakleen. Drivability symptoms can include rough idle, stalling, limp mode, bucking and sputtering, loss of power and, in some cases, trouble codes for emissions or traction control. It’s important to remember to let the engine get up to operating temperature before attempting any troubleshooting.

Honda’s cylinder deactivation has come with its share of problems. Even though the deactivated cylinders aren’t firing, they’re still creating a vacuum that can draw oil past the piston rings and oil control ring and up into the combustion chamber. Common issues include oil consumption, fouled spark plugs, misfires and even piston ring and catalytic converter damage. Drivers also report harshness and vibration due to an altered engine balance, wearing out hydraulic motor mounts prematurely. The oil burning and piston ring wear issues have even resulted in a class action lawsuit that Honda has had to follow up on, as well as numerous technical service bulletins. Coolant-sensor bypass devices are available to trick the engine management computer into shutting down the VCM feature and keeping all cylinders firing, compromising fuel economy in favor of engine longevity and smoothness.

The VCM system settlement covered Accord models (2008-2012), Odyssey models (2008-2013), Pilot models (2009-2013) and Crosstour models (2010-2012). As part of that settlement, Honda extended the powertrain warranty to eight years and unlimited mileage and reimbursed customers for out-of-pocket expenses related to diagnostics and repairs.

A separate lawsuit covers the 3.5L J35 V6 from model years 2016-2023 in models that include the Ridgeline, Pilot, Odyssey and Passport as well as the Acura MDX and TLX. This one stems from improperly ground crankshaft pins that can lead to premature bearing, piston and rod failure. Complaints have ranged from roughness to knocking, ticking, metal shavings in the oil filter and even complete engine seizure.

During the month of October, The Pronto Network will join independent auto repair shops across the United States in supporting the 2026 Brakes for Breasts fundraiser, an industry-wide effort raising funds for breast cancer vaccine research, the company announced.

As part of the fundraiser, participating Pronto Network Service Centers will provide customers with free brake pads or shoes. Customers pay for labor and any additional parts necessary to complete the brake job, and shops then donate 10% of the brake job directly to the Cleveland Clinic Breast Cancer Vaccine Research Fund, specifically supporting The Dr. Tuohy Lab and its breast cancer vaccine research. The Pronto Network says it will then match the donations made by these service centers.
Sponsoring Manufacturers and Partner Support
Additional sponsoring manufacturers participating in the fundraiser include Bendix, Bosch, DuraGo, NewTek, PowerStop, ProMax, and Wagner.

“We’re excited to bring the Brakes for Breasts fundraiser to a select group of our service centers this year,” said Kerri Gulick, director of marketing and communications for The Pronto Network. “Independent repair shops have strong connections to the communities they serve, and this fundraiser gives our network an opportunity to come together to support research that could have a meaningful impact on the future of breast cancer vaccines. In Part 1 of this double episode, learn how Zimbrick of Madison transformed its approach to ADAS calibration by bringing more of the process in-house. With three body shops, 16 automotive brands and a centralized glass and calibration center, Zimbrick partnered with National Calibration and Diagnostic Solutions (NCDS) and Autel to build a more controlled and scalable calibration workflow. The video explores how the right equipment, training and support can help collision repair facilities improve efficiency, documentation, repair quality and customer communication while keeping up with increasingly complex vehicle technology.
- Bringing ADAS calibration in-house: Zimbrick reduced its reliance on outside vendors to gain greater control over scanning, calibration and the overall repair process.
- Centralizing calibration services: A hub-and-spoke model allows three body shops to work with a centralized calibration center while maintaining consistent processes.
- Improving repair quality and accountability: In-house capabilities give Zimbrick greater visibility into technician training, OEM procedures, documentation and how calibrations are completed.
- Combining glass and calibration: Locating glass replacement and ADAS calibration together allows Zimbrick to complete more windshield installations and calibrations on the same day.
- Training the entire team: Education extends beyond technicians to estimators, helping staff better understand ADAS requirements and explain necessary procedures to customers.

- Building customer confidence: Employees can explain why a calibration is required, what equipment is being used and how the procedure fits into a complete repair rather than simply presenting an additional charge.

- Getting more from ADAS technology: Autel equipment provides diagnostic, calibration and documentation capabilities, while NCDS provides tooling recommendations, training, workflow guidance and ongoing technical support.

- Creating a scalable operation: With approximately 400 repair orders moving through the operation each month, bringing scans and calibrations under Zimbrick’s control helps turn a necessary repair procedure into an opportunity for greater efficiency and additional in-house service.
