The newly opened Allstate Auto Lab will allow claims specialists to observe repair technicians in a dedicated “negative-pressure” demonstration area, according to a press release.
Claims adjusters will also gain hands-on experience with 22 vehicles and four motorcycles, including electric, hybrid, and gas-powered models, the release adds.

The Auto Lab is housed inside Allstate’s Claims University, a 33,000-square-foot claims training center in Dallas, Texas, that opened in August. The university also includes a Property Lab where claims specialists learn about house claims.
Allstate says that the Auto Lab is designed using insights from more than 3.5 million auto claims and recreates scenarios customers experience most often.

“Today’s vehicles are far more complex than they were even a few years ago, and claims adjusters need a deeper understanding of how damage affects the entire vehicle,” said Mike Fiato, Allstate executive vice president and chief claims officer, in the release. “The Auto Lab allows them to build the expertise needed to help customers make informed decisions when they’re recovering from damage.”
The facility was designed to move training beyond classroom instruction by allowing employees to physically inspect the types of vehicles and damage they encounter in the field, the release states.
“Vehicle selection was guided by claims data and designed to reflect the most common types of claims, helping bring real-world repair situations into the learning environment,” the release states.
Claims adjusters examine the technologies, repair considerations, and damage patterns unique to each vehicle type, the release states.
Damage situations employees will train on include:
- “Collision damage, including front-corner, rear-end, side-impact and multi-vehicle accidents;
- “Hidden structural and undercarriage damage; and
- “Damage involving cameras, sensors and advanced safety systems.”

Allstate says the lab will prepare claims adjusters to evaluate modern vehicle damage and repair considerations. It adds this will help the adjusters provide more informed assessments and guidance to customers.
- “Inspecting 22 real damaged vehicles, including electric, hybrid, and gas-powered models, as well as four motorcycles.
- “Using a two-post lift to inspect undercarriage, structural components, and exhaust systems not visible from the exterior.
- “Engaging with diagnostic technology to identify damage to cameras, sensors, and ADAS.
- “Observing repair techniques in a dedicated negative-pressure demonstration area.”

The two-post lift will allow claims adjusters to inspect vehicles from underneath, providing a complete view of structural components, exhaust systems, and undercarriage damage that may not be visible from the exterior, the release states.

“The facility also includes a dedicated repair demonstration area where employees can observe repair techniques and gain a better understanding of how vehicles are restored,” the release states. “Advanced measuring technology helps illustrate structural movement and alignment issues that can influence repair needs, while the negative-pressure environment allows repair demonstrations to be conducted safely as learners observe the process.”
Seeing vehicle damage in person helps claims specialists create a “deeper understanding of how an accident affects the entire vehicle,” the release adds.

“The Auto Lab helps claims adjusters better understand the repairs necessary to return a vehicle to pre-damage condition,” according to the release. “That knowledge supports more informed damage assessments, stronger conversations with repair facilities, greater confidence in determining necessary repairs and clearer guidance for customers navigating the recovery process. As vehicles continue to evolve, the Auto Lab provides the infrastructure needed to keep training aligned with emerging technologies and repair practices.”

Allstate notes that electric vehicles and vehicles with ADAS require different repair and damage assessment considerations than gas-powered vehicles. It adds that damage to cameras, sensors, or blind-spot monitoring systems may not be visible from the exterior, but can “significantly affect repair needs and safety.”

“Allstate’s Auto Lab includes electric and hybrid vehicles specifically to train claims adjusters on these considerations, using the same diagnostic tools many repair facilities use,” the release states.
A lawsuit against State Farm alleging claim underpayment has been revived on appeal in New York.

State Farm argued it didn’t breach the policy in question because, under the policy terms, it paid the plaintiff based on its own repair estimate written at the prevailing competitive rate. Court documents state that State Farm determined the rate according to its own survey.
The New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department, unanimously reversed a lower court’s summary judgment in favor of State Farm.
The plaintiff, Prospect Auto Sales and Repairs, was given representative authorization by Janet Sukhram to repair her 2018 Audi Q7 and handle her claim with State Farm.
Sukhram executed an assignment of claim, assigning to the plaintiff all rights against the defendant for any damages from State Farm’s failure to pay for the total cost of the repairs.
As Sukhram requested, Prospect repaired the vehicle to its pre-accident condition for $19,736.60. However, State Farm paid the plaintiff $13,188.22 for the work, according to court documents.
In response, Prospect sued for breach of contract.
- “Had an obligation under the policy to indemnify Sukhram for the reasonable and necessary repairs made to the vehicle as performed by the repair facility of her choice;
- “Accepted full responsibility for payment for such repairs and entered into negotiations with the plaintiff regarding the specific cost of such repairs; and
- “Had a duty under Insurance Law § 2601 and Regulation 64, Part 216, and the policy to negotiate in good faith with the plaintiff to repair the vehicle.”

It adds that State Farm violated two New York laws — Insurance Law § 2601 (unfair claim settlement practices) and 11 NYCRR 216.7 (standards for prompt, fair, and equitable settlement of motor vehicle physical damage claims). Prospect contends that State Farm breached Sukhram’s policy by failing to negotiate with Prospect in good faith and pay in full for the repair procedures, parts, materials, and costs necessary to return the vehicle to its pre-accident condition.

State Farm argued for summary judgment to dismiss the suit, alleging that no private right of action exists under Insurance Law § 2601 and 11 NYCRR 216.7. Prospect opposed the motion. In April 2024, the Supreme Court granted State Farm’s motion.

“Contrary to the Supreme Court’s determination and the defendant’s contention, under a fair reading of the complaint, it does not set forth a cause of action to recover damages for violations of Insurance Law § 2601 and 11 NYCRR 216.7 but rather properly seeks to recover damages for breach of contract predicated, in part, on allegations of such violations,” the Appellate Court’s Sept. 23 order states. “Therefore, the court improperly granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the basis that there is no separate private right of action due to violations of Insurance Law § 2601 and 11 NYCRR 216.7.”
The court ruled that State Farm’s argument regarding the prevailing rate is “wholly conclusory and unsubstantiated, as the defendant never furnished the survey it purported to rely upon.”

“Further, to the extent an affidavit of the defendant’s representative submitted in support of the motion addressed the issue as to whether the defendant negotiated with the plaintiff in good faith regarding the procedures, parts, materials, and costs to return the vehicle to its pre-accident condition, the affidavit is not based on personal knowledge but rather improperly relies on hearsay within hearsay,” the order states.

In a separate case from 2024, Prospect sued State Farm on behalf of two of its customers over similar allegations to the Sukhram claim, and State Farm argued it paid its prevailing competitive rate of $100 for Tesla repairs. Prospect provided detailed estimates from at least nine other insurance companies who agreed to pay $125 an hour for Tesla repairs. State Farm sought summary judgment to dismiss the case. The Supreme Court of Westchester County in New York denied the motion.
In July 2025, Jay Sicht, Fender Bender and ABRN editor-in-chief, reported that 57% of 230 survey respondents said State Farm reduced the labor rates it offered their shop without explanation.
In November 2025, Society of Collision Repair Specialists (SCRS) Executive Director Aaron Schulenburg discussed the issue at a Collision Industry Conference (CIC) meeting.

Shops are seeing a shift from prevailing competitive rates to a rate the insurance company has defined as “reasonable,” he said. He said the insurance company is not defining “reasonable,” providing documentation justifying the reduction, or giving any indication of a valid statistical survey.

“Simply, ‘We’ve determined it’s enough, even though we’ve lowered it significantly from what we recognized before,’ it’s concerning,” Schulenburg said. “I think in some cases, the claim is that the data is coming from information providers who also claim not to be conducting labor rate surveys or even reporting on prevailing rates. But there’s no way to argue it, and there’s no way to document it because there’s no documentation provided to the industry.”

State Farm’s claims handling practices, including a shift to a centralized claim review process, labor rate reductions, and other claims practices, were a topic of contention with regulators and attendees during April’s industry events week in North Carolina.

SCRS Chairman Michael Bradshaw shared his experience with those carrier practice changes at his shop and noted the publication of a P&C Specialist article. He also mentioned he discussed the same carrier conduct and its effect on shops like his several months ago during a CIC open mic.

“We’ve seen a dramatic reduction in labor rates across the country,” he said. “This has been confirmed by article after article. …Over 60% of shops surveyed by Fender Bender said their rates had been reduced by State Farm in the last 12 months.

“Many times, we’re fearful of mentioning names and calling out the individuals that are engaging in the conduct… I can confirm it’s not market-specific; it’s not claim-specific. It is a very tactful approach that is being engaged in nationwide by the largest carrier in the country, State Farm…”

State Farm has been sued in several states over allegations that it systematically lowers actual cash values (ACVs) on total loss claims, including Tennessee, Arkansas, Alaska, Illinois, Kentucky, Mississippi, West Virginia, and North Carolina.
Cases in Kentucky and Mississippi were thrown out in October 2025. In April, State Farm agreed to settle the Arkansas class action suit for nearly $15.6 million.

U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) and Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) sent letters to executives of State Farm, Allstate, USAA, Farmers, Liberty Mutual, and American Family requesting information about an “unprecedented share of homeowners and auto insurance claims” that have been closed without payment to policyholders, according to a press release.

The letters follow a May Wall Street Journal (WSJ) article that found the five largest home insurers failed to pay more than 44% of claims resolved in 2025, up 36% from a decade ago. An August report from the newspaper found car insurers failed to pay 45% of auto liability and medical claims resolved last year, up from 35% a decade ago.

“The growing share of both homeowners and auto insurance claims resulting in no payment raises serious questions about whether consumers can trust their insurance companies to hold up their end of the bargain when disasters or emergencies occur and affect their most basic essentials: their home and car,” the senators jointly wrote. “While major insurance companies are raking in profits at record highs, a growing number of Americans are being left in financial ruin without the relief they paid for – in the wake of some of the worst moments of their lives.”
The letters individually list the 2025 profits for each of the companies:
- State Farm: Earned a net income of $12.9 billion, up $7.6 billion from 2024.
- Allstate: Earned a net income of $10.9 billion, up $5.6 billion from 2024.
- USAA: Did not disclose its 2025 earnings, but the letter says “the company tripled its profits from 2023 to 2024, earning $3.9 billion.”
- Farmers: Earned net income of $1.25 billion, more than double 2024’s ($588.6 million).
- Liberty Mutual: Earned net income of $6.79 billion, up 55% year over year.
- American Family: Earned annual net income of $3.1 billion, up 25% from 2024.

“Homeowners are typically required to purchase home insurance as a condition of their mortgage, while nearly every state requires drivers to maintain some form of auto liability coverage,” the senators write. “Homeowners and auto insurance help cover the cost of repairing a claimholder’s car or home, replacing belongings within them if they are damaged during a disaster or accident, or even paying for medical coverage if injuries are sustained during an accident.”
Auto insurance costs have surged, with average full-coverage premiums up 31% from 2023 to 2025, reaching $2,638 per year, including a 12% increase in 2025, the letter states.
The letter points to data from the Insurance Research Council, which found the share of uninsured drivers increased from 11.6% in 2019 to 15.4% in 2023.
The senators say homeowners insurance premiums increased 70% nationally between 2019 and 2025; for an average homeowner with $350,000 in rebuilding coverage, premiums increased 39%, or $760, in 2025.

“The record profits of insurance companies raise questions about whether increasingly aggressive claims-handling practices, including tactics to delay payments, are contributing to higher margins,” the letter states. “Indeed, insurance companies seem to be swimming in profits, with property and casualty insurers making a record $136 billion in 2025 and reporting the highest profitability from underwriting policies in 20 years.”
The letter requests that the insurers respond to the following by Oct. 16:

- “Provide your company’s yearly percentage and number of claim fulfillments and claims closed without payment for homeowners and personal auto insurance over the last 10 years, including: a. disaggregated for each type of peril your homeowners and personal auto insurance policies cover; and b. disaggregated by the reason for nonpayment, including claims that fell below the applicable deductible, were subject to a policy exclusion, were formally denied, were withdrawn by the policyholder, or resulted in no payment for any other reason.

- “For each year over the last 10 years, provide the number and percentage of homeowners and personal auto insurance claims that were initially denied or closed without payment that policyholders appealed or otherwise disputed, and the number and percentage of those claims for which your company subsequently made a payment or reversed its initial determination.

- “Explain the primary factors that have contributed to the increase in homeowners and personal auto insurance claims being closed without payment over the past decade and quantify the extent to which each factor (e.g., deductibles, policy exclusions, withdrawn claims, formal denials, or other reasons) has contributed to this trend.

- “Since 2015, has your company made any material changes to its homeowners or personal auto claims-handling policies, procedures, or guidelines? If so, describe those changes and the reasons for implementing them.

- “Describe any compensation, bonus, performance evaluation, or other incentive programs for your company’s employees, contractors, adjusters, or managers involved in homeowners or personal auto claims that incorporate metrics related to claim payments, claim severity, loss ratios, settlement amounts, claims closed without payment, or denial rates.

- “Describe your company’s use of artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, or other automated tools in the homeowners and personal auto claims process, including the safeguards in place to ensure fair and accurate claims determinations.
- “Will your company commit to providing this Committee and the public with its annual claims data, just like mortgage lenders report their loan data to the public?”
In April, Hawley sent a letter to State Farm’s CEO demanding the insurance company stop dragging its feet and pay policyholders in full for tornado damage that had happened a year prior.
Hawley notes that just days before the storm, a State Farm executive testified under oath before his subcommittee that the company pays its policyholders “promptly, courteously, and efficiently.”
“It is disappointing, but not surprising, that these words were an empty promise,” Hawley said.

During the subcommittee hearing, Hawley grilled Allstate and State Farm executives, saying testimony from adjusters and policyholders, along with previous lawsuits, appears to show the companies are “running a racket” and a “pattern of fraud” while making “outrageous profits.”
The Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs Subcommittee on Disaster Management, District of Columbia, and Census heard from two adjusters who testified that they were pressured to lower estimates.

In July, John Parese, a partner with Buckley, Wynne, and Parese, addressed the issue in a letter to Attorney General Pamela Bondi discussing insurance practices that harm consumers and the collision industry. The letter addressed the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs hearing.

“The unlawful practices exposed during that proceeding are virtually the same as those that occur every day with countless auto body repair claims,” the letter states. “Nearly every state auto body trade association has long advocated for greater consumer protections and for the protection of unlawful insurer practices.”

For years, Army recruiters have enjoyed flagging a special perk for new Advanced Individual Training graduates: an opportunity to return to their hometowns for 14 days with pay prior to their first duty station, with the understanding they’ll help local recruiters during that time and tell the Army story.
But according to the head of U.S. Army Recruiting Command, the new soldiers struggled to hold up their end of the deal.
The service’s decades-old Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program has been suspended, Lt. Gen. Johnny Davis confirmed at a forum hosted by the Association of the United States Army.
And while he said it’s being “looked at” for possible next steps, he also described the built-in problems keeping the service from getting its money’s worth.

“I would tell you, when the program was initiated and really delivered to the Army years ago and executed, that we had some good return on investment — about, you know, one or two percent,” Davis said in response to a question at the forum.

“But, bottom line, what we’ve learned over the years is that 20, 30,000 young superstars, when they were headed back home, were good; they got to go home,” he added. “But they weren’t really working with the recruiters as much as we wanted them to.”

Davis said leaders understood the “human element” of what was happening, in that new graduates were eager to reconnect with family and friends in what amounted to additional uncharged leave. But, he added, the Army had to consider what it was getting out of the arrangement.

Likewise, he said, the Army has in the past allowed National Guard and Reserve soldiers to return home for non-charged leave during the holiday break known as the Christmas Exodus on the understanding that they would support Army recruiting as ambassadors during that time.

“During that Christmas holiday, was there a lot of recruiters in the recruiting stations working with them? No,” Davis said. “So we’re really thinking through: is this return on investment, and is it worth the cost to the Army? Or can we take those funds and spend them in other ways to help our men and women.”
Davis said leaders were now “looking at other ways” to help soldiers get coveted hometown leave apart from the hometown recruiting program.
Army recruiting social media pages began discussing the suspension of the Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program in January, though the service has not publicly addressed the move until now.
HRAP dates to the 1980s. In its most recent form, soldiers had to be selected and approved for the program by a company commander.
In a 2022 Army news release, a recruiting center station commander in Missouri, Staff Sgt. Colton Dunbar, said the success of the program came down to “how the soldiers are leveraged.”

“We try to get the most out of them while they’re here by bringing them to the high school where they graduated and their communities to show everyone that this person was in your community six months ago as a civilian, but look at them now,” he said in the release. ”It helps to break down any barriers because they know that person in uniform — it helps show we are people just like everybody else.”
But from early on in the program, a lack of success metrics and specific service requirements have limited HRAP’s success.

A 1983 study from the U.S. Army Research Institute for the Behavioral and Social Sciences found that it was hard to evaluate the usefulness of program participants, because it was hard to track their impact outside of foot traffic to the recruiting office.
It also suggested, though, that there were nevertheless non-quantifiable benefits to having new soldiers present and visible in their hometown.

“Aides are credited for individuals they brought to the recruiter who subsequently enlist, but the total effect of the aide’s efforts is more subtle than the sum of their recruits,” the study found. “For example, aides can ‘plant seeds’ or lay the groundwork months in advance of an enlistment decision and receive no credit for an enlistment that occurs months after his or her departure.”
The Army hasn’t said when it will make final decisions on the way forward for HRAP.
